bugs.area: document / shape doc values (ShapeDocValues centroid; LatLonShapeDocValuesField and XYShapeDocValuesField getCentroid)
bugs.title: ShapeDocValues getCentroid returns (0, 0), far outside the shape's own bounding box, when the shape's total encoded length or area is zero (a line whose points coincide after encoding, or a polygon thinner than one encoding step)
bugs.summary: You build a doc-values shape with LatLonShape.createDocValueField or XYShape.createDocValueField and ask for its centroid; you expect getCentroid, documented as 'the centroid location for the geometry', to be a point of the shape, inside the bounding box that the same object returns. For a line whose points coincide after encoding (new Line({40, 40}, {-70, -70}), or two points closer than one encoding step) or a polygon thinner than one encoding step, Lucene returns Point(0.0, 0.0) instead, 7,500 km or more from the shape in these examples: the centroid is weighted by length or area, and when the total weight is zero the code skips the division and keeps the zero numerator. The other public factory, createDocValueField(name, createIndexableFields(name, line)), returns the real point for the same line.

bugs.area: geo / Tessellator cure step (polygon indexing for LatLonShape and XYShape, shape doc values)
bugs.title: Tessellator.cureLocalIntersections adds each triangle it cuts off twice, so LatLonShape and XYShape index that triangle twice and the shape doc-values centroid counts its area twice
bugs.summary: You index a polygon with LatLonShape or XYShape (createIndexableFields or createDocValueField) and expect each triangle of its tessellation to be stored once. When the Tessellator's cure step (cureLocalIntersections) cuts off a triangle to repair a small local self-intersection, it appends that same triangle twice (two identical tessellation.add calls at Tessellator.java:890 and:892, left by LUCENE-8620 in 8.3.0), so the shape carries one extra indexed triangle, ShapeDocValuesField.numberOfTerms is one too high and getCentroid counts that triangle's area twice; query results do not change. On its own the cure step fires only for self-crossing rings, which the javadoc excludes but the default checkSelfIntersections=false path accepts (for example POLYGON((6 3, 0 6, 4 0, 3 4, 5 1, 3 2, 6 3)), duplicated on every release from 8.3.0), and a valid polygon reaches it only when it already hits LFV-210 (a hole touching the shell), whose fix removes it.

bugs.area: spatial-extras / spatial4j bridge to spatial3d (Geo3dRectangleShape.reset), read by BBoxStrategy's value sources (BBoxValueSource: makeShapeValueSource, makeOverlapRatioValueSource)
bugs.title: Geo3dRectangleShape.reset(minX, maxX, minY, maxY) replaces the wrapped spatial3d box but keeps the old minX/maxX/minY/maxY, so with the Geo3d spatial context BBoxStrategy shape values report a stale box for every document and BBoxStrategy overlap-ratio relevance scores are wrong
bugs.summary: You use the Geo3d spatial context (Geo3dSpatialContextFactory) with BBoxStrategy and read each document's box with makeShapeValueSource or rank by makeOverlapRatioValueSource(queryBox,...), or you call reset(10, 20, 30, 40) on a Geo3d rectangle yourself. You expect reset to replace the whole rectangle (the spatial4j Rectangle.reset javadoc: 'Resets the state of this shape given the arguments'; spatial4j's own RectangleImpl.reset assigns all four bounds), so getMinX..getMaxY return 10, 20, 30, 40, the shape values return each document's indexed box, and a document box equal to the query scores 1.0, as it does with the default SpatialContext.GEO. Instead Geo3dRectangleShape.reset rebuilds only the wrapped GeoBBox and clears the center and bounding-box caches, never assigning the four fields that getMinX..getMaxY, getWidth, getHeight and getCrossesDateLine read: the rectangle equals rect(10, 20, 30, 40) but reports its previous bounds, BBoxValueSource (which creates one rect(0, 0, 0, 0) per segment and resets it for each document) reports (0, 0, 0, 0) for every document, and the self-overlap score is 0.0.

bugs.area: spatial-extras / SpatialStrategy recip-distance scoring (every strategy with a distance value source)
bugs.title: SpatialStrategy.makeRecipDistanceValueSource takes zScaling from half the corner-to-corner great-circle distance of the query's bounding box, which goes the short way round the globe once a geo box is wider than 180 degrees of longitude, so edge scores fall far below the documented ~0.1 (0.0082 for rect(-170,170,-10,10), 0.0028 for a 5S-5N band of all longitudes; released since 4.0.0)
bugs.summary: You score a geo spatial query with makeRecipDistanceValueSource, whose javadoc says zScaling is one tenth of the distance from the centre to the farthest edge, so scores run from 1 at the centre down to about 0.1 at the furthest edge. For a box wider than 180 degrees of longitude the method instead takes half the great-circle distance between the box's two opposite corners, and that distance goes the short way round the globe: for rect(-170,170,-10,10) zScaling is 1.41 instead of 17.0, and the edge point (170,0) scores 0.0082 instead of about 0.091 (for the band rect(-180,180,-5,5), 0.0028). Nothing fails; distance is over-weighted, so with FunctionScoreQuery.boostByValue a hit with inner score 10 at 170 degrees ranks below a hit with inner score 1 at 10 degrees on the band query, the reverse of the documented scaling.

bugs.area: spatial-extras / BBoxStrategy overlap-ratio relevance (BBoxOverlapRatioValueSource.score: intersection width when both boxes cross the dateline)
bugs.title: BBoxStrategy's overlap-ratio relevance (BBoxOverlapRatioValueSource) undercounts the overlap of two dateline-crossing boxes that intersect in two longitude pieces, so the score is too low
bugs.summary: You index a dateline-crossing rectangle with BBoxStrategy in the default geo context and score it with makeOverlapRatioValueSource and a query rectangle that also crosses the dateline, and you expect the documented score intersectionArea/queryArea*p + intersectionArea/targetArea*(1-p), where intersectionArea is 'the area of the intersection between the query and target envelopes'. When the two boxes wrap far enough round the globe that they overlap twice, once across the dateline and once on the far side (query rect(10,-170,-10,10) and document rect(170,20,-10,10) share 170..-170 across the dateline, 20 degrees, and 10..20, 10 degrees), the score counts only the piece across the dateline: 0.10317460317460317 instead of 0.15476190476190477 at p = 0.5. The both-cross branch computes the width as right - left + 360, which is only that piece, while the branch for one crossing box already adds up both pieces.

bugs.area: suggest / spell checking (DirectSpellChecker.suggestSimilar with a non-default StringDistance; FuzzyTermsEnum competitive-boost pruning)
bugs.title: DirectSpellChecker with a non-default StringDistance prunes candidates by comparing the metric's score with FuzzyTermsEnum boosts, so better candidates are never inspected (regression since 7.0)
bugs.summary: You give DirectSpellChecker a metric such as LevenshteinDistance or JaroWinklerDistance and expect what setDistance documents: candidates drawn from the term dictionary by Damerau-Levenshtein (the internal similarity), then ranked by your metric. Since 7.0 the code stores your metric's score in ScoreTerm.boost, a field documented as the internal similarity, and then skips later candidates and tells FuzzyTermsEnum to lower its edit distance by comparing their internal similarity with that number, which is on a different scale, so better terms are never looked at. With default settings, the index {lucen, lucena, lucenb, lucenc, lucend, lucenes} and the query 'lucene', LevenshteinDistance returns 'lucen' (0.833) instead of 'lucenes' (0.857), and with maxInspections=1 and the index {lucen, lucenes} all three shipped metrics return 'lucen' although 'lucenes' scores higher under the internal similarity and under each metric.

bugs.area: suggest / spell: SpellChecker.indexDictionary de-duplication (cached searcher vs. the new IndexWriter's index; clearIndex, swapSearcher)
bugs.title: SpellChecker.indexDictionary de-duplicates against its cached searcher instead of the index its new IndexWriter writes, so a rebuild with OpenMode.CREATE silently drops every word of the new dictionary that the old spell index already had (and after a failed searcher reopen, later calls drop words or index them twice)
bugs.summary: You build a spell index with SpellChecker.indexDictionary from the words {apple, banana}, then rebuild it from {apple, cherry}, passing an IndexWriterConfig with OpenMode.CREATE, which is documented as 'Creates a new index or overwrites an existing one'. You expect the spell index to hold apple and cherry. Instead it holds only cherry: the new writer starts from an empty index, but indexDictionary skips every word that its cached searcher of the old index still contains, so apple is silently dropped; the same stale check makes a call after a failed searcher reopen drop words (after clearIndex) or index them twice (on a retry).

bugs.area: suggest / SuggestStopFilter (query analysis of the analyzing and document suggesters)
bugs.title: SuggestStopFilter.end leaves out the positions of the stop words it removes at the end of the input (StopFilter counts them), so a suggester with SuggestStopFilter in its query analyzer returns extra suggestions for text that ends in removed stop words and a space (two or more stop words for AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester, one for the document suggester; wrong end since 4.5.0, visible in suggesters since 6.5.0)
bugs.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester over 'one direction' and 'one of the best' with a StopFilter index analyzer and a SuggestStopFilter query analyzer, as the SuggestStopFilter javadoc recommends, and look up 'one of the ' (the user has typed 'the' and a space). You expect what a StopFilter query analyzer gives, [one of the best], because the class is documented as 'Like StopFilter' except that it keeps an unterminated last stop word, and StopFilter adds the positions of removed trailing stop words to the final position increment in end. Instead SuggestStopFilter.end reports the input's own final increment (0 instead of 2), so the lookup automaton has too few trailing holes and the lookup also returns 'one direction'; the tokens and the final offset are correct.

bugs.area: analysis-common / Russian analyzer default stop words (RussianAnalyzer, snowball/russian_stop.txt; interaction with the Snowball RussianStemmer's ё-to-е fold)
bugs.title: RussianAnalyzer does not remove its default stop words when they are written with ё (её, ещё, всё, неё, чём): its StopFilter runs before the stemmer folds ё to е, although the bundled stop list says ё is translated to е
bugs.summary: You analyze Russian text with the stock RussianAnalyzer. Its default stop list, the bundled Snowball russian_stop.txt, says in its header that 'letter ё is translated to е', so it lists её, ещё, всё, неё and чём only as ее, еще, все, нее and чем, and since 9.0 the same analyzer without stop words maps the ё and е spellings of every word that reaches its stemmer to one term. But the StopFilter runs before the only step that folds ё to е (the Snowball RussianStemmer), so the е spellings are removed while the ё spellings pass the StopFilter and are indexed as е, ещ, все, не and чем: 'Он все еще читает книгу' gives [чита, книг] but 'Он всё ещё читает книгу' gives [все, ещ, чита, книг], with no error.
bugs.introduced_commit: 0203815ab2bf72a77fe8f58daa0e6e269e00e9a8 ('LUCENE-9220: regenerate all stemmers/stopwords/test data from snowball 2.0 (#1262)', apache/lucene-solr PR #1262 by rmuir; issue LUCENE-9220, now apache/lucene#10260) [read]. It regenerated org.tartarus.snowball.ext.RussianStemmer from Snowball 2.0, whose stem first replaces every U+0451 with U+0435; it did not touch RussianAnalyzer, and the 159 entries of russian_stop.txt are identical before and after. So the defect is an interaction: the chain order StopFilter before SnowballFilter and the analyzer's use of the Snowball list (imported by LUCENE-2206), whose header states the ё-to-е precondition, both date from LUCENE-2055 (a6b7c5552ba, rmuir, 2010-02-05, first released in 3.1.0); from 3.1.0 to 8.11.4 that precondition was already unmet, but the stemmer kept ё distinct for every word too, so stop words were treated like all other words. Nothing in the PR or issue discusses Russian or ё.

bugs.area: analysis-common / language analyzers (TeluguAnalyzer default stop set te/stopwords.txt, applied after IndicNormalizationFilter and TeluguNormalizationFilter)
bugs.title: TeluguAnalyzer runs its StopFilter after Indic and Telugu normalization, but its default stop list is not normalized, so 13 of the 43 single-word default stop words (for example కూడా, 'also') are never removed
bugs.summary: You analyze Telugu text with the stock new TeluguAnalyzer, whose default stop list (te/stopwords.txt) holds common function words such as కూడా ('also') that the analyzer should drop. The analyzer normalizes every token before its StopFilter and folds long vowel signs to short ones (ూ to ు, ీ to ి, ే to ె, ో to ొ), but the list holds only the unnormalized spellings, so the StopFilter sees కుడా and never matches the entry కూడా. As a result 13 of the 43 single-word default stop words are never removed and are indexed and searched as ordinary terms, while the Hindi analyzer, which has the same chain, ships the normalized forms in its list and removes all of its stop words.

bugs.area: analysis-common / Bengali analyzer default stop words (BengaliAnalyzer, bn/stopwords.txt; interaction with IndicNormalizationFilter and BengaliNormalizationFilter)
bugs.title: BengaliAnalyzer never removes 13 of its 116 default stop words (e.g. কারণ, শুধু, মধ্যে, অন্য) because its StopFilter runs after Indic/Bengali normalization while the bundled stopwords.txt has only unnormalized spellings

bugs.title: SoraniAnalyzer, LatvianAnalyzer and GalicianAnalyzer load the '#' comment lines of their bundled stopwords.txt as stop words: 60 of the 122 entries of SoraniAnalyzer.getDefaultStopSet, 9 of 170 for Latvian (including a bare '#') and 1 of 161 for Galician are comment text
bugs.summary: You call SoraniAnalyzer.getDefaultStopSet, LatvianAnalyzer.getDefaultStopSet or GalicianAnalyzer.getDefaultStopSet, documented as 'the default stop words set' built from the analyzer's bundled 'File containing default Kurdish/Latvian/Galician stopwords', and expect the stop words of that file; its '#' lines are comments, the format that about two dozen sibling analyzers load with the '#' comment marker and that StopFilterFactory's default 'wordset' format skips. Instead the three analyzers load the file with WordlistLoader.getWordSet(InputStream), which 'adds every line as an entry', so 60 of Sorani's 122 entries, 9 of Latvian's 170 (including a bare '#') and 1 of Galician's 161 are comment text such as '# set of kurdish stopwords', '# and' or '# galican stopwords'. The stock analyzers' tokens do not change, but code that lists, counts or reuses these sets sees the comments, and with a WhitespaceTokenizer the Latvian set removes a standalone '#' token ('lucene # search' gives [lucene, search]).

bugs.area: analysis / WordDelimiterGraphFilterFactory and WordDelimiterFilterFactory types option (parseTypes) versus the default WordDelimiterIterator character-type table
bugs.title: WordDelimiterGraphFilterFactory's types option (and the deprecated WordDelimiterFilterFactory's) refills the whole Latin-1 type table from getType instead of the filter's default table, so any rule, even one that restates a character's own type, silently changes how 8 other characters (¹ ² ³ ¼ ½ ¾ ª º) are tokenized
bugs.summary: You give WordDelimiterGraphFilterFactory a types file with one rule for a character that is not in your text (for example '$ => DIGIT', or even '- => SUBWORD_DELIM', which '-' already is) and expect every other character to keep the type it has without the option. Instead parseTypes fills all 256 Latin-1 entries from WordDelimiterIterator.getType (the Unicode general category), while the table the filter uses without the option is built from Character.isLowerCase/isUpperCase/isDigit; the two disagree on exactly 8 characters, so 'm² x³ 1½ ¼' analyzes to [m, ², x, ³, 1½, ¼] instead of [m, x, 1] and 'ªB' is no longer split. Nothing reports an error; a small change that seeds the Latin-1 entries from the default table fixes both factories.

The WordDelimiterGraphFilterFactory copy came with LUCENE-7619 (apache/lucene#8670, by GitHub mikemccand): branch_6x 4e4ec082caa7, master 637915b890d9 [read]. The two tables that disagree are older (Latin-1 table from the first WordDelimiterFilter, 148b4dbc923, 2006; the Character.getType switch with OTHER_NUMBER -> DIGIT and OTHER_LETTER -> ALPHA from SOLR-1078, 79414d2b726, 2009, used then only above the table); SOLR-2059 is the first change that types U+0000-U+00FF with getType. bugs.area: analysis-common / synonym.word2vec (Word2VecSynonymProvider.getSynonyms result cap; Word2VecSynonymFilter)
bugs.title: Word2VecSynonymProvider returns maxSynonymsPerTerm + 1 synonyms when the query term is not among its own k+1 HNSW hits (tied vectors or an approximate-search miss), so Word2VecSynonymFilter emits one synonym more than the documented maximum
bugs.summary: You configure Word2VecSynonymFilter with maxSynonymsPerTerm=k, whose javadoc calls it the 'maximum number of result returned by the synonym search', so you expect at most k synonyms per token. Word2VecSynonymProvider.getSynonyms searches the HNSW graph for k+1 neighbours on the assumption that the query term is always its own nearest neighbour, drops only the query term and never caps the result, so when the term is not among the hits it returns all k+1. With three terms that share one vector and k=1, getSynonyms(c) returns [a, b] and the filter emits 2 SYNONYM tokens; with 4000 distinct clustered vectors and the factory defaults, 4 terms get 6 synonyms because the approximate search with a beam of 6 does not reach the query term itself, although it is its own strict nearest neighbour by a margin of more than 0.03.

bugs.area: suggest / spell: SpellChecker.indexDictionary (n-gram spell index build)
bugs.title: SpellChecker.indexDictionary checks for already-indexed words only against the spell index as it was before the call, so a word that one dictionary repeats is indexed once per occurrence and suggestSimilar returns it several times, pushing distinct suggestions out
bugs.summary: You index a word list into SpellChecker with one indexDictionary call, and the list contains a word twice, for example a PlainTextDictionary with the lines relieve, relieve, receive. You expect each word to be indexed once, as indexDictionary already ensures for words that were in the spell index before the call, so suggestSimilar("recieve", 2) returns [relieve, receive]. Instead the duplicate check looks only at the spell index as it was before the call, so the repeated word is indexed twice and suggestSimilar returns [relieve, relieve], pushing receive out; the same words split over two calls are de-duplicated correctly.

bugs.area: suggest / spell: SpellChecker.suggestSimilar (index-based n-gram spell checker; comparator vs. full-queue accuracy cutoff)
bugs.title: SpellChecker.suggestSimilar with SuggestWordFrequencyComparator drops more frequent suggestions: once the queue is full it raises the accuracy cutoff to the score of the least frequent queued word, which is a valid bound only for a score-first order (since 3.1, LUCENE-2479)
bugs.summary: You build an index-based SpellChecker with the shipped SuggestWordFrequencyComparator ('Frequency first, then score') and ask for suggestions restricted to a field, expecting the most frequent qualifying words among the retrieved candidates. Once the queue holds numSug words, suggestSimilar raises its accuracy cutoff to the score of the queue's head, which under this comparator is the least frequent queued word, so a later candidate that is more frequent but scores slightly lower is rejected before its frequency is even read. With 'receive' in 50 documents and one-edit neighbours such as 'relieve', 'reprieve' and 'retrieve' in one document each, suggestSimilar('recieve', 1, reader, field, SUGGEST_WHEN_NOT_IN_INDEX) returns [relieve] instead of receive (numSug 1-3 all leave it out; numSug 4 ranks it first).

The commit added the Comparator constructor, setComparator, SuggestWordScoreComparator and SuggestWordFrequencyComparator and built the queue with the comparator, but left the full-queue cutoff unchanged. The cutoff itself comes from the 2004 sandbox import 57cd0765650 ('min=((SuggestWord) sugqueue.top).score'), when the only order was score then frequency and the cutoff was a valid lower bound; later commits on those lines only renamed or reformatted them (895f763d214 2006, 3619c380d6f LUCENE-1968 insertWithOverflow, 5b83cc59b2e LUCENE-1257 generics, 1620366b5ca LUCENE-2608 min renamed to the accuracy parameter, 4c724b958b1 SOLR-2257 term-text tie-break in both comparators, 2cbf261032d LUCENE-9570 reformatting). bugs.title: WordBreakSpellChecker.suggestWordBreaks drops better suggestions when maxChanges >= 3: the full-queue early return added in 9.12.0 (GITHUB#12100) assumes a breadth-first order that the depth-first recursion does not follow
bugs.summary: You index some words and call WordBreakSpellChecker.suggestWordBreaks with setMaxChanges(3) or more, and you expect the maxSuggestions splits of the term that rank best by Lucene's own order (fewest breaks, then highest frequency). No error is raised, raising maxChanges from 3 to 4 makes the answer worse, and 9.11.1 returns the right split.

bugs.area: queries / MoreLikeThis query construction (MoreLikeThis.createQuery truncation at IndexSearcher.getMaxClauseCount)
bugs.title: MoreLikeThis keeps the lowest-scoring selected terms when the query reaches the boolean clause limit, so the truncated query silently drops the most interesting terms (regression since 4.10.0)
bugs.summary: You let MoreLikeThis select more terms than the global boolean clause limit, for example setMaxQueryTerms(2000) on a long text under the default limit of 1024, and call like(...). You expect the query, which createQuery deliberately truncates to the clause limit instead of failing, to keep the 1024 most interesting (highest tf*idf) of the selected terms, as it did up to 4.9.1. Instead createQuery pops its queue lowest score first and stops at the first TooManyClauses, so the query holds the 1024 lowest-scoring selected terms and none of the best ones (in the repro, 0 of the 76 top words survive).

It bounded the term queue to min(maxQueryTerms, #terms), flipped it from highest-first (FreqQ.lessThan 'fa > fb') to lowest-first ('a.score < b.score') and removed createQuery's own maxQueryTerms stop, but kept createQuery's pop-and-break-on-TooManyClauses loop, which dates from the first MoreLikeThis check-in (7952217cea6, 2005-01-17) and was correct only for a best-first queue; the issue thread (9 comments) never mentions the pop order or the clause limit. bugs.area: analysis / hunspell (Hunspell.spell compound checking)
bugs.title: Hunspell spell-checker: CHECKCOMPOUNDTRIPLE misses an x|xx triple letter (one letter before the boundary, two after) at the second and later boundaries of a compound, so words such as operabareeel (opera + bare|eel) are accepted (absolute break position compared with the tail's relative length)
bugs.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary with CHECKCOMPOUNDTRIPLE, which hunspell(5) defines as 'Forbid compounding, if compound word contains triple repeating letters (e.g. foo|ox or xo|oof)', and expect Hunspell.spell to reject a compound with a triple letter at any boundary, as C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 do and as Lucene's own checkcompoundtriple fixture requires for bareeel (bare|eel). Instead Lucene rejects bareeel but accepts operabareeel, barebareeel and foobareeel (opera, bare or foo + bare|eel), and with the public Swedish dictionary (sv_SE) it accepts sommarmusikradiooomskuren while it rejects musikradiooomskuren. The cause: Hunspell.mayBreakIntoCompounds receives an absolute break position (the tail's offset in the word plus the relative break) but tests 'breakPos < length - 1' against the tail's relative length, so at the second and later boundaries the x|xx half of the check is skipped whenever the absolute break position is at least the tail length minus 1, while the xx|x half ('breakPos > offset + 1') is offset-aware and still works.

bugs.title: Hunspell spell skips the per-entry checks on COMPOUNDRULE compound parts, so it accepts compounds that C Hunspell rejects: a KEEPCASE first part in capitalized or upper case, a FORCEUCASE last part in lower case, and a NEEDAFFIX or FORBIDDENWORD entry as a first or middle part
bugs.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary that joins foo/G and bar/H by 'COMPOUNDRULE GH', give foo or bar one of the per-entry flags KEEPCASE, FORCEUCASE, NEEDAFFIX or FORBIDDENWORD, call Hunspell.spell, and expect the answer C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 give (and Lucene itself gives when the same parts are joined by COMPOUNDFLAG): Foobar and FOOBAR rejected when foo is KEEPCASE, foobar rejected when bar is FORCEUCASE, and foobar rejected when foo is a NEEDAFFIX virtual stem or a FORBIDDENWORD entry. Instead spell returns true in all four cases, with and without -ea, in every release since 8.9.0; on the public Swedish dictionary sv_SE it accepts lower-case rule compounds such as tolvkronorsgatan that the dictionary's FORCEUCASE flag and C Hunspell reject. The cause: checkCompoundRules takes every non-final part as a raw dictionary.lookupWord result, without the NEEDAFFIX, FORBIDDENWORD, COMPOUNDFORBIDFLAG and first-part case (KEEPCASE) filters, and checkLastCompoundPart never applies the FORCEUCASE check (hasForceUCaseProblem) that the COMPOUNDFLAG path uses.

bugs.area: analysis / hunspell (Dictionary FLAG UTF-8 parsing under the SET encoding)
bugs.title: Hunspell Dictionary with FLAG UTF-8 and an 8-bit SET other than ISO8859-1 silently merges UTF-8 flags that share a lead byte, so spell and the stemmer accept forms the dictionary forbids (some SET values fail to load instead)
bugs.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary whose affix file says FLAG UTF-8 (flags are UTF-8 characters) and SET ISO8859-2, KOI8-R, microsoft-cp1251 or another 8-bit encoding except ISO8859-1, with two suffix classes whose flags are, say, U+00E1 and U+00E2, and expect what C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 do on the same bytes: a word that carries only the first flag takes only the first suffix. Instead Lucene reads the flags from text already decoded with the SET charset, so each 2-byte flag becomes two characters and an affix rule keeps only the first one, the shared lead byte: both classes merge, spell accepts the forbidden forms (kote, lasa in the repro) and the stemmer returns kot for kote, with no error. Only no SET, SET ISO8859-1 and SET UTF-8 work; ISO8859-14 merges too (its decoder reports ISO-8859-1 as its charset, and the re-encode turns remapped flag bytes into '?'), and with ISO8859-3, -6 or -8 the load throws UnmappableCharacterException because a flag byte is unassigned in that charset.

bugs.area: analysis-stempel / egothor stemmer trie reductions (Optimizer, Optimizer2; Compile tool, Trie.reduce)
bugs.title: Stempel: running Optimizer or Optimizer2 on an already merge-reduced trie silently corrupts it, because Optimizer.optimize remaps references to rows it has not placed yet to row 0
bugs.summary: You build a stempel table with the Compile tool and a method string that has two merge passes (for example '-M22' or '-0ME22'), or you call reduce(new Optimizer2) (or Optimizer) on a table that a merge pass already reduced, such as a loaded table; Optimizer2's javadoc says its row joining keeps the stemmer able to 'recognize words for which the original trie was built', so the training words should keep their stems, as they do after one pass. Instead the second pass silently corrupts the trie: two Optimizer2 passes over the one-word trie {aab -> Da} lose its only entry, Compile '-22' stems every training form of a small table to null and '-M22' leaves every form unstemmed (while '-2' and '-M2' are correct), and one more Optimizer2 pass over the bundled Polish table changes 8,356 of 21,147 keys whose whole path is stored. The cause is Optimizer.optimize (inherited by Optimizer2): it walks the rows from the highest index down and remaps every child reference through a remap array that is still 0 for rows it has not placed yet, which is only correct when every child has a higher index than its parent; a freshly built trie has that property, but the output of a merge pass does not (shared rows, self-loops, pre-order renumbering).

bugs.area: analysis/stempel / egothor stemmer table serialization (Row.store vs Row(DataInput); Gener, Compile 'G', StempelStemmer.load)
bugs.title: Stempel's Row.store writes the count of all cells but skips the empty ones, so a stemmer table reduced with Gener (Compile method letter G) fails to load with EOFException or loads misaligned and gives wrong stems
bugs.summary: You compile a stemmer table with the stempel Compile tool using a method string that contains G (Gener, the reduction that drops infrequent commands), or reduce a trie with Gener and store it, and expect StempelStemmer.load to read the table back and stem like the trie that was stored. Instead Row.store writes the number of all cells of a row and then skips the empty cells (no command and no reference) that Gener leaves behind, so Row(DataInput) reads too many cell records and runs into the next row: usually load fails with java.io.EOFException (Compile -0ME2G, -0M2G and -0MEG on an 11-lemma Polish table, -EG on a 20-line table, the bundled table reduced with Gener, which then has 38,322 empty cells), and sometimes the table loads without error but answers wrongly (Compile G on a 4-line dictionary: for 'walked' the expected patch is Db and the loaded table gives null). Writing getCells, the existing count of the non-empty cells, fixes it in one line and changes no byte of any table without empty cells, such as the bundled table and every table compiled without G.

bugs.area: analysis / hunspell (Hunspell.spell and suggest compound checking, CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN replacements)
bugs.title: Hunspell spell-checker: a CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN simplified compound form (the optional replacement field) after the first compound part is checked from the start of the whole word, so valid compounds such as dampfschiffahrt (dampf + schiff|fahrt with 'ff f ff') are rejected and some words (schiffschiffahrt, or auu with 'u u u') make spell/suggest throw StackOverflowError (expandReplacement returns offset 0 over an array that still holds the earlier parts)

Instead Lucene accepts schiffahrt but rejects dampfschiffahrt and donaudampfschiffahrt (and barfozar, barfur and barbozan on the content of its own checkcompoundpattern2/3 fixtures), and spell/suggest throw StackOverflowError for schiffschiffahrt, for 'auu' with the one-word dictionary au and 'CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN u u u', and for words of native Hunspell's own checkcompoundpattern4 (Telugu sandhi) fixture. The cause: CheckCompoundPattern.expandReplacement builds the expanded word from the start of the whole word (word.chars[0.. word.offset + breakPos], which keeps the earlier compound parts for the FORCEUCASE check) but returns it as a CharsRef with offset 0, while its callers index it relative to the current part, so at the second and later boundaries the stem lookup starts at the beginning of the word and the remaining tail never gets shorter.

bugs.title: Hunspell: the part of an affix condition that overlaps the strip is checked with java.util.regex without escaping the dash, so a bracket such as [a-c] there means the range a..c instead of the set {a, -, c} that hunspell(5) defines, and the rule is applied or dropped wrongly

Instead Lucene's Hunspell.spell accepts ax and rejects ay (likewise xa and ya for the PFX twins on ba), and HunspellStemFilter stems ax to ab and leaves ay unstemmed. bugs.area: monitor / query decomposition (QueryDecomposer.decomposeBoolean)
bugs.title: Monitor's QueryDecomposer ignores minimumNumberShouldMatch=1 when a BooleanQuery has one required clause and no usable SHOULD clause, so Monitor.match reports queries that match nothing
bugs.summary: You register with the Monitor a BooleanQuery that has one required clause and minimumNumberShouldMatch=1 but no SHOULD clause that can match, for example 'topic AND at least one of [list]' built from an empty list, (+text:alpha)~1. Core Lucene defines this query to match nothing (BooleanQuery.rewrite returns MatchNoDocsQuery and IndexSearcher counts 0 hits), so you expect the Monitor never to report it. Instead the default QueryDecomposer keeps such a query whole only when minimumNumberShouldMatch > 1 and otherwise replaces it by its lone required clause (plus its MUST_NOT exclusions), which the Monitor runs as the final matcher, so Monitor.match reports the query for every document containing alpha, for example 'alpha beta'.

bugs.area: monitor / read-only query index (ReadonlyQueryIndex.purgeCache refresh)
bugs.title: A read-only Monitor's purgeCache returns without refreshing when another refresh is running, so a query committed before the call can stay invisible after it returns
bugs.summary: You open a read-only Monitor over a query index that a writable Monitor updates, register and commit a new query with the writer, and call purgeCache on the read-only Monitor, whose javadoc says read-only users 'MUST call it when you want new changes'. You expect the new query to match once the call returns. Instead, if another refresh of the same Monitor (its own background refresh, or another thread's purgeCache) is already running and has read the older commit, purgeCache calls the non-blocking SearcherManager.maybeRefresh, which returns false at once, drops that result and still notifies the onPurge listeners; the running refresh then installs the older commit, so the new query is still unmatched after both have returned, until some later refresh.

bugs.area: monitor / query decomposition and match scoring (QueryDecomposer Set<Query> parts, ScoringMatch/ExplainingMatch resolve)
bugs.title: Lucene Monitor's QueryDecomposer collects a query's parts in a Set, so a sub-query that occurs more than once in a registered query (a repeated SHOULD or MUST clause, or a term shared by two nested disjunctions) is scored once by ScoringMatch and ExplainingMatch instead of once per occurrence
bugs.summary: You register a query such as '(red apple) (green apple)' or 'apple apple' in a Monitor and match the document 'red green apple' with ScoringMatch or ExplainingMatch, expecting the score the query itself gives that document, which is what IndexSearcher returns, because BooleanQuery counts a repeated clause at every occurrence (0.5230583 and 0.26152915). Instead the Monitor reports 0.39229372 and 0.13076457: the default QueryDecomposer collects the query's parts in a Set, which keeps equal parts once, and the scoring matchers add up the scores of the distinct parts, so the shared 'apple' is counted once. Which queries match is not affected; only the scores and explanations of such queries are too low.

bugs.area: monitor / HighlightsMatch hit set (Hit.compareTo used as TreeSet identity)
bugs.title: Monitor HighlightsMatch drops a hit when another hit has the same positions but different offsets (for example shingles or multi-word synonyms), because HighlightsMatch.Hit.compareTo ignores offsets
bugs.summary: You register a query such as wi OR "wi fi" (or the prefix query wi*, or guinea OR cavy with a 'guinea pig => cavy' synonym rule) in a Monitor whose analyzer stacks tokens at one position, match a document with HighlightsMatch.MATCHER, and expect both hits that Weight#matches reports: for 'wi fi' with ShingleFilter(2,2) and unigrams these are 0(0)->0(2) for 'wi' and 0(0)->0(5) for 'wi fi'. Instead HighlightsMatch keeps only one of them and getHitCount is 1, because Hit.compareTo compares start and end positions only and the hits are kept in TreeSets, which treat compareTo == 0 as a duplicate, although Hit's own equals (a record over all four fields) says the two hits differ. Which hit survives depends on clause order, and the same root cause makes getHits(field).contains(...) ignore offsets and lets HighlightsMatch.equals return true for two objects whose hashCodes differ.

bugs.area: analysis-common / Thai (ThaiCharFilter.read single-pass look-ahead; the 'thai' char filter factory and the default ThaiAnalyzer as consumers; new in 10.6.0)
bugs.title: ThaiCharFilter tests its multi-character rules (double Sara E, decomposed Sara Am, tone mark before an above/below vowel) on the raw look-ahead characters, before its own zero-width removal and deduplication have run on them, so a zero-width character or a repeated tone mark inside such a pattern leaves the anomaly in the output and the default ThaiAnalyzer merges the word with its neighbours
bugs.summary: You index Thai text with the default ThaiAnalyzer, which runs ThaiCharFilter before the tokenizer, and expect a word typed with two of the typos the filter documents fixing (ที่ with its tone mark typed twice and before the vowel, ท่่ี, or แมว written as two Sara E with an invisible zero-width joiner between them) to be indexed like the clean word, because the filter's javadoc says it removes zero-width characters, deduplicates repeated tone marks, reorders a tone mark typed before an above/below vowel, joins double Sara E and recomposes decomposed Sara Am precisely so that the BreakIterator does not merge adjacent words. ThaiCharFilter makes one pass and tests its multi-character patterns against the raw next characters, while zero-width removal and deduplication act only on the character at the front of its buffer, after the earlier character has already been emitted, so the output still holds the tone-before-vowel, double Sara E or decomposed Sara Am sequence (ท่ี, เเมว, ทํา), which a second pass of the same filter would clean. The BreakIterator then merges words: ฉันทำงานท่่ีบ้าน is indexed as [ฉัน, ทำ, งาน, ที่บ้าน] instead of [ฉัน, ทำ, งาน, บ้าน], ฉันรักเ + ZWJ + เมวมาก as [ฉัน, รักแมวมาก], and a TermQuery for บ้าน or แมว finds 0 documents.

bugs.area: analysis-common / Thai (ThaiNormalizer.normalize rule order; ThaiNormalizationFilter, the 'thaiNormalization' factory and the default ThaiAnalyzer as consumers; new in 10.6.0)
bugs.title: ThaiNormalizer looks for a decomposed Sara Am before it converts Lakkhangyao or removes an extra tone mark, so its output can still be the decomposed form (Nikhahit + tone + Sara Aa), and the default ThaiAnalyzer indexes น้ำ ('water') typed with two tone marks inside a decomposed Sara Am as a different term
bugs.summary: You index Thai text with the default ThaiAnalyzer (or ThaiNormalizationFilter) in which the word น้ำ ('water') is typed with a decomposed Sara Am and an extra tone mark inside it, น + Nikhahit + Mai Ek + Mai Tho + Sara Aa, and you expect the term น้ำ, because ThaiNormalizer documents that it recomposes Nikhahit + tone + Sara Aa into Sara Am and (per its code comment and upstream test) keeps the last of two different tone marks. ThaiNormalizer tests for the decomposed Sara Am in one forward pass over the raw characters, before it converts a following Lakkhangyao and before its last step removes the extra or repeated tone mark, and it never checks again, so the output is นํ้า (U+0E19 U+0E4D U+0E49 U+0E32), still the decomposed form; a query for น้ำ misses the document, while a second normalize call, or the same two tone marks typed in the other order, gives น้ำ. When the token filter runs without ThaiCharFilter, ท + Nikhahit + Lakkhangyao likewise gives ทํา instead of ทำ, and a doubled tone mark inside the decomposed form gives นํ้า.

bugs.area: analysis / common miscellaneous (ConditionalTokenFilter#end and OneTimeWrapper#end: final position increment on the delegate branch)
bugs.title: ConditionalTokenFilter (ProtectedTermFilter, CustomAnalyzer when/whenTerm) reports a final position increment of 0 when the last token went through the wrapped filters, so a trailing hole from upstream (such as a removed trailing stop word) is lost and the next value of a multi-valued field starts one position too early (since 7.4.0)
bugs.summary: You analyse 'abc the' with WhitespaceTokenizer, a StopFilter that removes 'the', and a ProtectedTermFilter that wraps a LowerCaseFilter (or the CustomAnalyzer equivalent whenTerm(...).addTokenFilter("lowercase").endwhen), and expect end to report the removed stop word as a final position increment of 1, as the same chain does without the condition and as the class itself does when the last token is protected ('x the' gives 1). Instead it reports 0 whenever the last token went through the wrapped filter, although LowerCaseFilter never touches positions: end keeps the wrapped chain's end state, and the internal wrapper that feeds that chain resets the increment to 0. In a multi-valued field ['abc the', 'def'] with the default gap 0, 'def' is then indexed at position 1 instead of 2, so the PhraseQuery "abc def" matches the document (1 hit) where the plain chain gives 0 (executed).

bugs.area: analysis / common miscellaneous (ConcatenatingTokenStream#incrementToken and #end: carry-over of child final position increments)
bugs.title: ConcatenatingTokenStream loses a source's trailing position increment (for example a removed stop word) when the next source produces no tokens, so later tokens are indexed too close and phrase queries over-match
bugs.summary: You build one field from several token streams with ConcatenatingTokenStream, for example the values 'alpha the', '' and 'beta', each run through a StopFilter that removes 'the'. You expect the hole left by the removed 'the' to survive, as it does when no empty value sits in between and as IndexWriter keeps it for the same values in a multi-valued field, because LUCENE-8650 (7.7.0) made the class carry each source's final position increment over to the next token. Instead each exhausted source overwrites the pending increment instead of adding to it, and end reports only the last source's own increment, so a source with no tokens erases the hole: 'beta' is indexed directly after 'alpha', the exact phrase "alpha beta" matches this document but not the single value 'alpha the beta', and with an empty last source end reports 0 instead of 1.

bugs.area: analysis-common / ConcatenateGraphFilter and ConcatenateGraphFilterFactory (custom tokenSeparator)
bugs.title: ConcatenateGraphFilter treats a custom tokenSeparator as its internal one-byte separator label: an ASCII separator is doubled wherever it already occurs inside a token ('e-mail' becomes 'e--mail'), and a non-ASCII separator fails an assertion with -ea or is written as one truncated byte with -da (U+2013 becomes U+0013, U+00B7 a lone 0xB7 byte, i.e. invalid UTF-8)
bugs.summary: You join tokens with ConcatenateGraphFilter (or the concatenateGraph factory) and a custom tokenSeparator, and expect what the javadoc says, every token joined with that separator: the single token 'e-mail' stays 'e-mail', 'e-mail' and 'x' joined with '-' give 'e-mail-x', and 'new' and 'york' joined with U+2013 give the UTF-8 bytes of new, U+2013, york. Instead the filter passes the custom separator to an escaper written for its internal one-byte label U+001F, so every occurrence of an ASCII separator inside a token is doubled ('e--mail', 'e--mail-x', and 'new york' for a keyword token with a space separator). A non-ASCII separator fails the escaper's assertion with -ea and, with -da, is cut to its low byte: U+2013 gives 'new' U+0013 'york', and U+00B7 gives the invalid UTF-8 term [6e 65 77 b7 79 6f 72 6b].

bugs.area: suggest / document (NRT) suggester (ContextSuggestField context validation; the context then passes through ConcatenateGraphFilter's SEP_LABEL escaping and HOLE removal)
bugs.title: ContextSuggestField accepts contexts that contain U+001E or U+001F although its javadoc promises an IllegalArgumentException for reserved characters; the completion analysis then drops U+001E (a suggestion indexed under context 'a<U+001E>b' is stored as, returned for and labelled with the exact context 'ab') and doubles U+001F (context 'a<U+001F>b' never matches its own exact query and is reported as 'a<U+001F><U+001F>b')
bugs.summary: You index one suggestion under context 'ab' and another under context 'a<U+001E>b' with ContextSuggestField, and expect an IllegalArgumentException, because the constructor javadoc says it throws one 'if value or contexts contains any reserved characters' and U+001E and U+001F are exactly the characters that SuggestField and CompletionQuery reject as reserved (or, at the least, a context that round-trips). Instead both documents are indexed: ContextQuery.addContext("ab") returns both and reports both with context 'ab', addContext("a<U+001E>b") returns nothing, and a context 'a<U+001F>b' is also accepted, its exact query returns nothing and addAllContexts reports it as 'a<U+001F><U+001F>b'. The cause: ContextSuggestField.validate checks a context only for U+001D (CONTEXT_SEPARATOR); the context then goes through ConcatenateGraphFilter, which turns a U+001E byte into an epsilon and escapes U+001F by doubling it, while ContextQuery builds its automaton from the raw characters, so the index side and the query side disagree.

bugs.area: suggest / analyzing suggester (AnalyzingSuggester FST input encoding: analyzed form + END_BYTE 0x00 + dedup byte, inherited by FuzzySuggester; Util.TopNSearcher result path)
bugs.title: AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester do not escape the 0x00 byte that ends each analyzed form, so a U+0000 in a suggestion or key makes them return the same suggestion twice, lose the EXACT_FIRST exact match, or return entries that do not start with the key
bugs.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester (or a FuzzySuggester) with its default constructor and KeywordAnalyzer from two entries, 'cat' with weight 1 and 'cat\u0000\u0000s' with weight 5, and call lookup('cat', 5); you expect each entry once with the exact match 'cat' first, which is what you get when the second entry uses U+0001 instead of U+0000. Instead you get [cat/1, cat\u0000\u0000s/5, cat/1]: the suggester stores each entry as its analyzed bytes, then a 0x00 end marker, then a dedup byte, without escaping a 0x00 that belongs to the text, so the stored input of 'cat' is a prefix of the stored input of 'cat\u0000\u0000s', and the FST top-N search returns 'cat' a second time through a path that skips the suggester's duplicate filter. The same collision makes lookup('foo\u0000') return 'foo' and lets a longer U+0000-extended entry take the EXACT_FIRST exact-match slot.

It created AnalyzingSuggester with the FST input 'analyzed bytes + END_BYTE 0x00 + dedup byte', escaping only 0xff (then SEP_LABEL) inside the analyzed bytes, and with the EXACT_FIRST rule 'an END_BYTE arc leaving the node reached by the key is an exact match' [read]. The design was first written on the unreleased feature branch lucene3842 in bc0d717c8f6 (2012-09-23, 'LUCENE-3842: get escaping working; fix exactFirst to mean exact surface form'), which was squash-committed to trunk as f2f91bae46c. Second step: LUCENE-4534 (2537836d4ab trunk / a299cc65772 branch_4x, 2012-11-05, 'handle 0 byte values in lookup keys') made dictionaries whose analyzed forms contain 0x00 buildable (decoded sort comparator) but kept the encoding, which exposed the duplicate and EXACT_FIRST symptoms [exec]. Both steps are in 4.1.0, the first release of the API.

bugs.area: suggest / analyzing suggester (AnalyzingSuggester.build failure atomicity: hasPayloads is published before the new FST; inherited by FuzzySuggester)
bugs.title: AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester take the new input's payload flag before build can fail, so after a failed rebuild (or during a rebuild) lookups decode the previous FST in the wrong payload format: the payload glued to the suggestion text, or the suggestion returned as the payload
bugs.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester (or FuzzySuggester) from input with payloads, for example 'foo' with weight 10 and payload 'p1', then rebuild the same instance from a dictionary without payloads whose input throws an IOException partway through, and you expect lookups to keep returning the previous build ('foo', payload 'p1') or nothing. Instead lookup('fo') returns the text 'foo<U+001F>p1' with payload null, because build stores the new input's payload flag at its start (AnalyzingSuggester.java:394) but replaces the FST only at its end (:589-590), so the old FST is read with the new flag; in the opposite direction (old build without payloads, failed rebuild with payloads) lookups return empty text with 'foo' as the payload, or trip the suggester's own assertion with -ea. A lookup made while such a rebuild is still reading its input sees the same mixture, and store writes it to disk, so load brings it back.

bugs.area: classification / Naive Bayes classifiers (CachingNaiveBayesClassifier, SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier vs SimpleNaiveBayesClassifier, BM25NBClassifier)
bugs.title: CachingNaiveBayesClassifier and SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier offer and assign the empty class term '', which SimpleNaiveBayesClassifier and BM25NBClassifier skip, so the Naive Bayes classifiers disagree on the same index
bugs.summary: You index training documents where some carry an empty class value (for example StringField("cat", "") for unlabelled rows) and build SimpleNaiveBayesClassifier, CachingNaiveBayesClassifier and SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier on the same reader, expecting the two subclasses to offer the same classes as their parent, which (like BM25NBClassifier) skips the empty class term with 'if (next.length > 0)'. Instead the caching and document classifiers list '' as a class: getClasses('car') gives ['', 'fruit', 'vehicle'] against the parent's ['fruit', 'vehicle'], and with two empty-class 'car bus' documents both assign '' to 'car bus' where the parent assigns 'vehicle'. Their class loops (CachingNaiveBayesClassifier.reInitCache and SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier.assignNormClasses) lack the parent's length check; whether the fix adds it there or removes it from the parent and BM25NBClassifier is open.

bugs.area: analysis/stempel / egothor stemmer trie reductions (Trie.reduce with Lift and Gener; the shared PolishAnalyzer.getDefaultTable table)
bugs.title: Stempel's Trie.reduce with Gener or Lift rewrites the cells of the trie it is given, so reducing PolishAnalyzer.getDefaultTable, documented as unmodifiable, silently changes the stems of every later PolishAnalyzer and StempelPolishStemFilterFactory in the JVM

Instead Lift.optimize and Gener.optimize take the input's own row list and rewrite its cells in place (Lift moves commands up a level and clears references, Gener drops infrequent commands and references) before copying them into the result, so the input answers differently afterwards: after PolishAnalyzer.getDefaultTable.reduce(new Gener) every new PolishAnalyzer stems 'książkami rzekami pracowali' to [książk, rzekami, pracowali] instead of [książek, rzekść, pracować], and a one-key trie {aa -> Da} reduced with Lift(false) starts to answer getLastOnPath('a') = Da instead of nothing. bugs.area: analysis / kuromoji romanization (ToStringUtil.getRomanization; JapaneseReadingFormFilter romaji mode)
bugs.title: Kuromoji's romaji reading (ToStringUtil.getRomanization, used by JapaneseReadingFormFilter with useRomaji=true) writes the small tsu ッ as a doubled consonant only before the k, s, t and p rows and silently drops it before any other kana, so loanwords with ッ before g, z/j, d, b or h/f lose it: バッグ 'bag' and バグ 'bug' both become 'bagu', ベッド becomes 'bedo'
bugs.summary: You analyze Japanese text with JapaneseTokenizer and JapaneseReadingFormFilter(useRomaji=true), whose romanizer is documented as 'Romanize katakana with modified hepburn', and expect the small tsu ッ to double the next consonant, as the method already does for キット -> 'kitto' and マッチ -> 'matchi'. bugs.title: TeluguNormalizer composes ఒ + ౌ (U+0C12 LETTER O + U+0C4C VOWEL SIGN AU) into AU (U+0C14) but never applies its own AU -> OO fold to the result, so in a chain without IndicNormalizationFilter in front the two spellings of AU normalize to different terms

bugs.area: analysis / kuromoji and nori Viterbi unknown-word length cap (JapaneseTokenizer and the 'japanese' factory; KoreanTokenizer, KoreanAnalyzer and the 'korean' factory)
bugs.title: JapaneseTokenizer and KoreanTokenizer cut an unknown word at the 1024-char cap (MAX_UNKNOWN_WORD_LENGTH) even in the middle of a surrogate pair, so a supplementary character (an emoji, a CJK Extension B ideograph) at char 1023 of a long same-class run is emitted as two unpaired surrogate halves and indexed as U+FFFD
bugs.summary: You analyze a long run of text that kuromoji or nori treat as one unknown word, for example 1,200 chars of Thai without spaces through the 'japanese' tokenizer, or 400 x (U+1F441 U+FE0F) emoji through the default KoreanAnalyzer, and the run holds an emoji or a rare ideograph such as U+20000; you expect every term to consist of whole characters, as it does when that character sits one position earlier or later. Instead both tokenizers stop the unknown word at exactly 1024 UTF-16 chars without checking for a surrogate pair, so when the character's first half is char 1023, term 0 ends in a lone high surrogate and term 1 starts with the lone low surrogate. The index silently stores both halves as U+FFFD, and in the unigram modes a TermQuery for the character finds 0 documents instead of 1.

bugs.area: analysis / kuromoji and nori Viterbi tokenizers, discardPunctuation (ja.ViterbiNBest.isPunctuation and its three discard sites, ko.Viterbi.shouldFilterToken)
bugs.title: JapaneseTokenizer and KoreanTokenizer with discardPunctuation=true (the default) keep punctuation and symbols outside the BMP (U+10100, U+1E95E, emoji such as U+1F600) as tokens, because isPunctuation classifies a single UTF-16 unit (the high surrogate), while BMP characters of the same general category are dropped (released since 3.6.0 and 7.4.0)
bugs.summary: You tokenize '日本 😀 日本' or '한국 𐄀 한국' (U+1F600, U+10100) with JapaneseTokenizer or KoreanTokenizer and discardPunctuation=true, the default, and expect [日本, 日本] and [한국, 한국], because the javadoc says punctuation tokens are dropped and both tokenizers drop every BMP character of the same Unicode general category (Po U+3001, So U+2605, Sm U+2207). Instead the supplementary character is kept as a token ([日本, 😀, 日本], [한국, 𐄀, 한국]): isPunctuation(char) calls Character.getType on the high surrogate alone, whose type is SURROGATE, so the discard test at the token start never sees the real category. No error is raised; the default KoreanAnalyzer indexes the extra token, and the default JapaneseAnalyzer removes it only later, through its part-of-speech stop filter, which leaves a position gap.

bugs.area: analysis / ICU (DefaultICUTokenizerConfig syllable rules MyanmarSyllable.rbbi / MyanmarSyllable.brk, used for Myanmar text when myanmarAsWords=false; ICUTokenizerFactory 'icu' with myanmarAsWords="false")
bugs.title: ICUTokenizer with myanmarAsWords=false silently drops the Myanmar modifier letters U+A9E6 and U+AA70 (Shan and Khamti reduplication, as in 'ကꧦ'), and Common-script letters such as MICRO SIGN that fall into a Myanmar run, because MyanmarSyllable.rbbi gives a token status only to syllables and numbers
bugs.summary: You tokenize Myanmar-script text with ICUTokenizer in syllable mode (new DefaultICUTokenizerConfig(true, false), or ICUTokenizerFactory with myanmarAsWords="false"), whose only documented effect is that Myanmar text 'will be tokenized as syllables', and expect every letter to end up in some token, as in the default mode, where 'ကꧦ' (KA + U+A9E6 MYANMAR MODIFIER LETTER SHAN REDUPLICATION) gives [ကꧦ] and 'ကꩰ' (KA + U+AA70 MYANMAR MODIFIER LETTER KHAMTI REDUPLICATION) gives [ကꩰ]. Instead syllable mode gives [က] for both, a mark on its own gives no token, and 'ကောင်း µm' gives [ကောင်း, m] (the space and µ are Common script, so the script iterator keeps them in the Myanmar run), all without an error. The cause is the rule file: MyanmarSyllable.rbbi gives a non-zero rule status only to syllables built on a consonant, consonant placeholder or independent vowel ({200}) and to numbers ({100}), and ICUTokenizer skips every segment with status 0.

bugs.area: analysis / UAX29URLEmailTokenizer JFlex URL rules (FTPurl production; analysis-common)
bugs.title: UAX29URLEmailTokenizer does not emit an ftp URL with no path ('ftp://host') as one URL token, although its http rule and RFC 1738 make the path optional
bugs.summary: You run text such as 'get it from ftp://ftp.example.com today' or 'ftp://localhost' through UAX29URLEmailTokenizer, whose javadoc says URLs are 'tokenized according to the relevant RFCs', and expect each ftp URL as one <URL> token, because RFC 1738 (section 3.2.2: 'The whole url-path may be omitted, including the "/" delimiting it') and RFC 3986 (an empty path after an authority) allow it, and the same tokenizer already keeps 'http://localhost' whole. Instead it emits 'ftp' as <ALPHANUM> followed by the rest on its own ('ftp.example.com' as <URL>, 'localhost' as <ALPHANUM>, '192.0.2.10' as <NUM>, '//anonymous@ftp.example.org' as <EMAIL>), because the grammar's FTPurl rule makes the '/'-led FTPorFILEpath mandatory while the http rule beside it makes its path optional. With a trailing slash ('ftp://ftp.example.com/') the URL is one token, and nothing reports an error.

bugs.area: analysis-common / util CSVUtil (CSV line parsing for the kuromoji user dictionary and the kuromoji/nori dictionary builders)
bugs.title: CSVUtil.parse decodes every quoted field except the last one of the line, so a quoted last field (for example the part-of-speech of a kuromoji user-dictionary entry) keeps its quote characters
bugs.summary: You parse a CSV line whose last field is quoted, for example CSVUtil.parse("x," + CSVUtil.quoteEscape("To be, or not to be")), or load a kuromoji user dictionary written with every field quoted, and expect the quoted value to be decoded the same way as in any other position, as parse does for every field followed by a comma. Instead the last field comes back raw, enclosing quotes and doubled inner quotes included: parse("\"a,b\",\"c,d\"") returns [a,b, "c,d"], and the dictionary line "abcd","a b cd","foo1 foo2 foo3","bar" yields tokens whose part-of-speech is "bar" with the quotes. The cause is one line: parse passes each comma-terminated field through unQuoteUnEscape (CSVUtil.java:56) but adds the final field as sb.toString (:65).

bugs.area: analysis-common / util CSVUtil (CSV line parsing for the kuromoji user dictionary and the kuromoji/nori dictionary builders)
bugs.title: CSVUtil.parse keeps the enclosing quotes of a field that holds both a comma and a double quote, so it does not decode CSVUtil.quoteEscape output
bugs.summary: You encode a value that holds both a comma and a double quote with CSVUtil.quoteEscape, which doubles the quotes and wraps the value in quotes (the exact output Lucene's own TestCSVUtil.testQuoteEscapeQuotesAndComma expects), put it before another field in a CSV line, and expect CSVUtil.parse to give the value back, as it does for values with only a comma or only a quote. Instead parse unescapes the inner quotes but keeps the enclosing ones: the value a "b", c is encoded as "a ""b"", c" and parse returns "a "b", c" with the outer quotes still on it. The cause is the unquote regex ^"([^"]+)"$ (CSVUtil.java:29), which strips enclosing quotes only from a field that has no quote inside.

bugs.area: analysis / kuromoji system dictionary builder (ja.dict.TokenInfoDictionaryEntryWriter reading and pronunciation length bytes; TokenInfoMorphData decoding; custom dictionaries built with DictionaryBuilder)
bugs.title: Kuromoji's DictionaryBuilder silently accepts a reading or pronunciation of 128 or more chars and stores its length in 7 bits, so the built system dictionary returns an empty or truncated reading and a garbage pronunciation (a too-long base form, by contrast, is rejected)
bugs.summary: You build a custom kuromoji system dictionary with DictionaryBuilder from an IPADIC-format CSV that has a row whose reading is 128 katakana chars long (or, more naturally, a 64-char proper noun with a 136-char reading), and you expect either an IllegalArgumentException at build time, as the builder throws for a stored base form of 16 or more chars that its compact format cannot hold, or the reading back unchanged. Instead the build succeeds, because putEntry writes each length as (byte) (length << 1 | kanaFlag) with no check, so the stored length is the real length mod 128: getReading and JapaneseTokenizer's ReadingAttribute return "" for the 128-char reading and only the first 8 chars of the 136-char one, a 128-char pronunciation comes back empty, a pronunciation stored after a wrapped reading is decoded from the reading's own bytes (a 4-char pronunciation came back as the single char U+0304), and JapaneseReadingFormFilter indexes the empty or truncated reading as the term.

bugs.title: Nori's DictionaryBuilder checks that rows sharing a left context id have the same part of speech only with a Java assert, so with assertions off a custom system dictionary silently gives those words the part of speech of another row and KoreanPartOfSpeechStopFilter drops or keeps them wrongly
bugs.summary: You compile a custom nori system dictionary with DictionaryBuilder from MeCab-format rows in which the noun 가 (NNG) and the particle 는 (JX) share left context id 1, and expect the builder either to reject the source (the compiled format keeps only one part of speech per left id, and kuromoji's builder throws 'Multiple entries found for leftID' for the same case) or each word to keep its own part of speech. Instead, with assertions off, the builder overwrites the single slot for left id 1 with the part of speech of the row it writes last, because the only check is an assert (TokenInfoDictionaryEntryWriter.java:100): 가 then reports left POS JX, and KoreanTokenizer followed by KoreanPartOfSpeechStopFilter with DEFAULT_STOP_TAGS returns no token instead of [가]. With -ea the build fails with a bare AssertionError rather than an IllegalArgumentException that names the problem.

bugs.title: Flexible StandardQueryParser narrows out-of-range int literals with intValue, so i:[2147483648 TO *] matches every document with the field

bugs.area: core / document (DateTools date-to-string term encoding: timeToString/dateToString and stringToTime/stringToDate)
bugs.title: DateTools strings stop sorting by date and stop round-tripping outside years AD 1..9999: the 'yyyy' year-of-era pattern drops the BC era (2 BC sorts after AD 1 and parses back as AD 2; 1 BC and AD 1 give the same string) and gives years after 9999 a fifth digit (10000 sorts before 2026, and stringToTime throws ParseException on DateTools' own output)
bugs.summary: You convert a date before AD 1 or after 9999 with DateTools.timeToString (or dateToString) and expect what the class javadoc promises: strings whose lexicographic order is date order, which stringToTime turns back into the same time. Instead the SimpleDateFormat pattern 'yyyy...' prints the year of era with no era and at least four digits: 2 BC-01-01 becomes "00020101", which sorts after AD 1's "00010101" and parses back as AD 2-01-01 (at YEAR resolution 1 BC and AD 1 both give "0001"), and 10000-01-01 becomes "100000101", which sorts before "20260101" and makes stringToTime throw ParseException, because the parser is chosen by string length. Range queries, prefix queries and sorts on such terms therefore return wrong results with no error.

bugs.area: queryparser / classic and flexible date ranges (QueryParserBase.getRangeQuery, TermRangeQueryNodeProcessor; setTimeZone and ConfigurationKeys.TIMEZONE)
bugs.title: QueryParser.setTimeZone (and StandardQueryParser.setTimeZone) is used only to round the inclusive end of a date range to 23:59:59.999; both dates are still parsed in the JVM default time zone, so with a non-default zone d:[6/1/2005 TO 6/4/2005] covers a shifted window and exclusive ranges ignore the setting
bugs.summary: You give the query parser a time zone with setTimeZone (plus setLocale and setDateResolution) and parse d:[6/1/2005 TO 6/4/2005], expecting what the QueryParser javadoc promises, a range 'between 2005-06-01 and 2005-06-04', read in that zone: June 1 00:00 to June 4 23:59:59.999 there. Instead both dates are parsed by a DateFormat that still uses the JVM default zone, and only the rounding of the inclusive end to 23:59:59.999 uses the configured zone, so the window starts at midnight in the JVM zone and ends at the end of the configured-zone day that contains the JVM-zone midnight of June 4: with the JVM on UTC and the parser on New York the June 4 New York documents are silently lost (and May 31 from 20:00 matches), with the JVM on UTC and the parser on Tokyo the first nine hours of June 1 are lost. Exclusive ranges such as {6/1/2005 TO 6/4/2005} ignore the configured zone entirely, and the classic and the flexible parser behave the same.

bugs.area: search / phrase matching (ExactPhraseMatcher, SloppyPhraseMatcher and PhrasePositions position arithmetic; PhraseQuery.Builder and MultiPhraseQuery.Builder accept the positions)
bugs.title: The phrase matchers add a document position and a query position offset in int: with an offset near 2^31 an exact PhraseQuery or MultiPhraseQuery loops forever inside one document (IndexSearcher#setTimeout does not stop it) and a sloppy one returns false hits
bugs.summary: You build a PhraseQuery with term a at position 0 and term b at position Integer.MAX_VALUE (the builder accepts it, because it only checks that positions are >= 0 and in order) and count it on a one-document index whose text is 'x a b'. You expect 0 hits, because no indexed position can be that far from a. Instead the exact matcher adds a's document position 1 and b's offset Integer.MAX_VALUE in int, the sum wraps to a negative number, both of its advance steps then leave its state unchanged, and IndexSearcher#count never returns, even with a 1 s IndexSearcher#setTimeout; with slop 1 the same kind of overflow makes the sloppy matcher return the document 'b x x a' as a hit.

bugs.area: highlighter / original Highlighter, QueryScorer and WeightedSpanTermExtractor (phrase-to-span conversion)
bugs.title: Highlighter with the default QueryScorer returns no fragment for a matching PhraseQuery or MultiPhraseQuery that has a position hole (for example a removed stop word) and a slop within the number of holes of Integer.MAX_VALUE: WeightedSpanTermExtractor converts it to a SpanNearQuery with the plain int sum slop + positionGaps, which wraps to about Integer.MIN_VALUE, so the span query matches nothing
bugs.summary: You analyse 'the quick brown fox jumps' with a stop-word analyzer, search for the phrase "quick the fox" with slop Integer.MAX_VALUE (for example from the user text "quick the fox"~3000000000, which the classic QueryParser turns into "quick ? fox"~2147483647; the query matches), and highlight the hit with Highlighter and QueryScorer, expecting 'the quick brown fox jumps', which slop Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 or the same phrase without the hole gives. Instead getBestFragment returns null, with no error: WeightedSpanTermExtractor rewrites the phrase as new SpanNearQuery(clauses, slop + positionGaps, inorder) with a plain int sum, the removed stop word counts as one position gap, the sum wraps to -2147483648, and a span query with that slop accepts no match, so no term is marked. bugs.area: highlighter / vectorhighlight BaseFragListBuilder (FastVectorHighlighter, SimpleFragListBuilder, WeightedFragListBuilder)
bugs.title: FastVectorHighlighter with fragCharSize = Integer.MAX_VALUE (or any value above Integer.MAX_VALUE - spanStart) returns the whole field with only the first match highlighted: BaseFragListBuilder computes spanStart + fragCharSize in int, the sum wraps negative, and every later match is silently dropped (SimpleFragListBuilder, the default, and WeightedFragListBuilder)
bugs.summary: You index the field 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa foo bbb foo ccc foo ddd' with term vectors (positions and offsets), search foo, and call FastVectorHighlighter.getBestFragments with fragCharSize = Integer.MAX_VALUE to get the whole field, expecting 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa foo bbb foo ccc foo ddd', which fragCharSize 1000 or Integer.MAX_VALUE - 100 gives. Instead you get 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa foo bbb foo ccc foo ddd', with no error: BaseFragListBuilder.createFieldFragList computes the fragment end as spanStart + fragCharSize in int, where spanStart is the first match's start minus the 6-char margin (15 here), so the sum wraps negative and the fragment closes at the end of the first match. The fragment is then re-centred to [0, Integer.MAX_VALUE), which covers the whole field, and every later match is discarded.

bugs.area: highlighter / classic Highlighter fragmenting (SimpleSpanFragmenter.isNewFragment position counter; Highlighter.getBestTextFragments)
bugs.title: Classic Highlighter's SimpleSpanFragmenter splits a short phrase match across two fragments because its position counter lags the real token positions: the Highlighter never shows it the first token or tokens that overlap the previous one, so the phrase is recognised one or more words late and getBestFragment can return only half of it
bugs.summary: You highlight 'Lucene is a search library written in Java' with the classic Highlighter, a QueryScorer for PhraseQuery 'search library', the default StandardAnalyzer and SimpleSpanFragmenter(scorer, 20), whose javadoc says it 'breaks text up into same-size fragments but does not split up Spans', and expect the 14-character phrase to stay in one fragment. Instead the fragments are 'Lucene is a search' | ' library written in Java' and getBestFragment returns 'Lucene is a search'; the same cut happens at the default fragment size 100 whenever the size threshold falls at the phrase's second word, and after a leading stop word or a word split by WordDelimiterGraphFilter the lag grows to two positions, so even three-word phrases are cut. The fragmenter counts positions only from the tokens the Highlighter shows it, and the Highlighter never shows it the first token or tokens that overlap the previous one, so it recognises the phrase one or more words late.

bugs.title: Classic Highlighter's SimpleSpanFragmenter.start does not reset waitForPos, so a Highlighter reused for the next text (or for the same text again) keeps suppressing fragment boundaries after a phrase match that ended the previous text: one oversized fragment, then one-word fragments and a different best fragment, depending on what was highlighted before

Hits and scores are unaffected; only the snippet layout changes, and it depends on what the same Highlighter highlighted before.

bugs.area: highlighter / UnifiedHighlighter default summary (FieldHighlighter.getSummaryPassagesNoHighlight over the SplittingBreakIterator that splits multi-valued fields on MULTIVAL_SEP_CHAR)
bugs.title: UnifiedHighlighter's no-match summary of a multi-valued field counts the internal U+0000 value separator as a passage, so the summary contains a NUL character and shows one value or sentence fewer than requested
bugs.summary: You store two values in one field ('First value.' and 'Second value.'), run a query that matches the document but not that field, and ask the UnifiedHighlighter for 2 passages; you expect the documented default summary, the first 2 sentences from the field (for example 'First value.... Second value.', the way the highlight path joins values). Instead you get 'First value.\u0000': the highlighter joins the values with an internal U+0000 separator, its SplittingBreakIterator reports a boundary on both sides of that character, and FieldHighlighter.getSummaryPassagesNoHighlight turns the 1-character gap into a passage, so the NUL is returned and takes the second value's slot (3 passages give 'First value.\u0000Second value.'). With an empty first value even 1 passage returns just '\u0000'.

bugs.area: highlighter / classic Highlighter formatters (GradientFormatter, SpanGradientFormatter)
bugs.title: GradientFormatter and SpanGradientFormatter reverse the colour gradient on every channel where the min colour is larger than the max colour, so with the javadoc's own white-to-black example the top-scoring term is drawn white

bugs.area: highlighter / classic Highlighter fragmenting (SimpleSpanFragmenter.isNewFragment; Highlighter.getBestTextFragments)
bugs.title: Classic Highlighter's SimpleSpanFragmenter splits a phrase match across fragments when two phrases overlap, when a longer phrase shares a shorter one's start (the result then depends on clause order), or when the phrase starts on stacked synonyms: it protects only the first span that starts at the current position, skips the span lookup while it waits for a span to end, and never sees a span that starts on a token the Highlighter does not show it
bugs.summary: You highlight a text with the classic Highlighter, a QueryScorer and SimpleSpanFragmenter, whose javadoc says it 'breaks text up into same-size fragments but does not split up Spans', for a query with two overlapping phrases ('new york' OR 'york city hall'), two phrases that share a start ('new york' OR 'new york city hall'), or a phrase whose words get synonyms stacked on them by SynonymGraphFilter, and you expect every phrase match shorter than the fragment size to stay inside one fragment. Instead the fragmenter cuts inside the longer phrase ('The museum is near New York City' | ' Hall and the park', 'We flew to New York City' | ' Hall last week', 'I left my big laptop' | ' bag on the train'), so getBestFragment can return only part of the phrase, and in the same-start case listing the longer phrase first in the BooleanQuery makes the phrase come out whole. Hits, scores and which words are highlighted are correct; only the fragment boundaries are wrong.

bugs.area: highlighter / UnifiedHighlighter re-analysis without a searcher (highlightWithoutSearcher: MemoryIndexOffsetStrategy reader == null branch + WEIGHT_MATCHES)
bugs.title: UnifiedHighlighter.highlightWithoutSearcher returns the text with no highlights under its default flags (WEIGHT_MATCHES) when the query also has a required or filter clause on another field
bugs.summary: You build a UnifiedHighlighter without a searcher (builderWithoutSearcher, default flags) and call highlightWithoutSearcher("body", query, "a b c", 1) with +title:x +body:a or +body:a #year:[2000 TO 2030], expecting 'a b c', which highlight gives for the same text on an indexed one-document copy, which the same call gives with withWeightMatches(false), and which 8.x gave by default. Instead it returns 'a b c' with no mark: under WEIGHT_MATCHES the whole query's Weight#matches runs on a MemoryIndex that holds only the highlighted field, where the other-field clause cannot match, so Matches is null ('doc doesn't match') and the highlighter falls back to the unmarked summary. The searcher path answers other-field clauses from the real index (OverlaySingleDocTermsLeafReader); the no-searcher branch has no such view, so a clause it cannot evaluate is treated as false.

bugs.area: highlighter / UnifiedHighlighter stored-value loading (LimitedStoredFieldVisitor maxLength cut)
bugs.title: UnifiedHighlighter cuts a stored value at maxLength UTF-16 units even between the two halves of a supplementary character (an emoji, a CJK Extension B ideograph), so the snippet can end in an unpaired high surrogate, for example 'Hello \uD83D'

bugs.summary: You give the UnifiedHighlighter a CustomSeparatorBreakIterator('.'), alone or inside LengthGoalBreakIterator, and expect passages to start and end at the breaks its own next reports, just after each '.'. Instead following and preceding are off by one next to the separator: on 'Aa bb. Cc dd. Ee ff' (breaks 0, 6, 13, 19) following(5) returns 13 instead of 6 and preceding(13) returns 13 instead of 6, so a min-length-6 summary is 'Aa bb. Cc dd.' instead of 'Aa bb.' and the phrase 'dd ee' is shown as 'dd. Ee ff' instead of ' Cc dd. Ee ff'. Nothing throws and the match is still highlighted; only the snippet boundary moves by one segment.

bugs.area: analysis / opennlp OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator (java.text.BreakIterator implementation, next(int))
bugs.title: OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator.next(n) returns DONE instead of the end of the text when the n-th boundary is the last one, so next(1) differs from next and a caller that steps with next(n) until DONE loses the final sentence group
bugs.summary: You set a text on an OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator and call next(n) to jump n sentence boundaries, expecting the n-th boundary, as java.text.BreakIterator#next(int) promises ('Returns the nth boundary from the current boundary') and as n calls of next give. When that boundary is the end of the text, next(n) returns DONE (-1) instead: with the model-free NLPSentenceDetectorOp on 'Whole text is one sentence.', next from first returns 27 but next(1) returns -1, and on the module's three-sentence test text (boundaries 0, 31, 59, 102) next(3) from first returns -1 instead of 102 while next(2) correctly returns 59. The iterator is still moved to the end, so only the returned value is wrong; code that steps with next(n) until DONE loses the final sentence group.

bugs.area: analysis-opennlp / OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator (public java.text.BreakIterator over OpenNLP sentence spans: setText, previous, following, moveToSentenceAt)
bugs.title: OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator on text that starts with whitespace: a backward walk with previous returns a non-boundary and then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and following at an offset inside the leading whitespace throws StackOverflowError, because setText keeps the sentence detector's whitespace-trimmed first sentence start while first and next use the text's begin index
bugs.summary: You create an OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator, give it a text that starts with whitespace, for example ' Sentence number 1 has 6 words. Sentence number 2, 5 words.', and walk it backward with last/previous (the reverse loop shown in the BreakIterator javadoc), expecting the forward boundaries [0, 33, 60] in reverse order and then DONE. Instead previous returns 2, which is not a boundary, and the next previous throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (Index -1); following(0) on a one-sentence text with leading whitespace recurses until StackOverflowError. The OpenNLP sentence detector trims whitespace from its spans and setText stores those starts unchanged, so the first stored sentence start lies after the begin index that first and next treat as the first boundary.
