It brought the pending-delete set, the synchronized deletePendingFiles that retries over a copy (new HashSet<>(pendingDeletes)), the retry from every mutating call and the revive in createOutput/renameFile without that monitor; line origins in the branch: 8cd731be50a, 85c546b742b, 24f55abfd50, plus f8bd22e58c9 on master. The createOutput path was masked in 6.2.0-7.3.1 by LUCENE-6171 (CREATE_NEW; 45d2d2e7d34 / a893c645952) and re-opened in 7.4.0 by LUCENE-8275 (#9322; 9f4e6c5da8d / aa341476fdb), which made the revive delete the old file before creating the new one; LUCENE-8318 (#9365; b178321bd1b / 3fe612bed20, 7.4.0) fixed only the single-threaded re-add and left the race unchanged

bugs.area: store / NativeFSLockFactory (write.lock: in-JVM LOCK_HELD guard and cross-process mutual exclusion)
bugs.title: NativeFSLockFactory tracks the write locks this JVM holds by real-path string instead of by file, so obtaining write.lock through a second path to the same file (a hard link, or a bind mount of the index directory) opens and closes a second channel on it, which silently drops the holder's OS lock while its ensureValid keeps passing and lets an IndexWriter in another process open and commit to the same index
bugs.summary: In one JVM you hold an index's write.lock (an open IndexWriter on directory A) and then, in the same JVM, open the same lock file through another real path: a bind mount of A at a second path, or a hard-link copy of A's files that includes write.lock, opened with IndexWriter, CheckIndex or addIndexes(Directory...). You expect that second open to fail with LockObtainFailedException while the first writer keeps its lock, so that a writer in another process on A is refused, as the IndexWriter javadoc promises. Instead the second open gets past NativeFSLockFactory's in-JVM check (LOCK_HELD compares toRealPath strings, which differ), opens a second FileChannel, gets OverlappingFileLockException and closes that channel, which on Linux drops the process's lock on the file; the first lock still passes ensureValid, a writer in another process then opens A and commits, and the first writer's next delete-only commit replaces that commit (on main: 'expected:<REFUSED> but was:<OBTAINED>' and 'the other process's acknowledged commit (doc 'child') was replaced by this writer's commit').

The class itself came three days earlier in 70472ad2cdf2 (r464611), whose in-JVM guard (a static factory map keyed by the canonical lock directory) was path-keyed too; neither commit was released on its own. Not a regression: the path key was never replaced by a file identity. bugs.area: misc / store: HardlinkCopyDirectoryWrapper#copyFrom hard-link path (against the core/store Directory#copyFrom and FilterDirectory#copyFrom contracts; reached through core/index IndexWriter.addIndexes(Directory...))
bugs.title: HardlinkCopyDirectoryWrapper.copyFrom unwraps both directory chains to the innermost FSDirectory and hard-links there, so every FilterDirectory in between is skipped for the copied file: an inner TrackingDirectoryWrapper does not record it, an inner LockValidatingDirectoryWrapper does not check its lock, and a one-sided byte-transforming or namespace-owning layer is bypassed
bugs.summary: You wrap an FSDirectory in TrackingDirectoryWrapper (or LockValidatingDirectoryWrapper, or your own FilterDirectory), wrap that in HardlinkCopyDirectoryWrapper, and copy a file in with copyFrom or IndexWriter.addIndexes(Directory...). You expect the copy to pass through the wrapped directory, as createOutput through the same wrapper does: on main Directory#copyFrom says 'Any per-file bookkeeping performed by createOutput must also cover copied files', and FilterDirectory#copyFrom names this class as one that delegates to in.copyFrom. Instead copyFrom unwraps both chains to the innermost FSDirectory and hard-links there, so no layer in between runs: getCreatedFiles stays , the copy succeeds after the inner write lock was released, and a byte-transforming layer on one side reads back the raw bytes (through addIndexes, a committed index that cannot be opened), with no error at copy time.

bugs.area: store / NRTCachingDirectory (Directory write-once contract)
bugs.title: NRTCachingDirectory.createOutput does not throw FileAlreadyExistsException when the name already exists in its other home (RAM cache vs wrapped directory), so the file ends up in both homes: deleteFile then leaves the other copy listed and readable, and close fails and, with assertions disabled, loses the file
bugs.summary: You wrap a directory in NRTCachingDirectory, write a file with IOContext.DEFAULT (it goes to the wrapped directory), and then call createOutput again for the same name with a small flush context (which goes to the RAM cache), or the other way round. You expect FileAlreadyExistsException, which the Directory contract requires for any existing name. Instead the second create succeeds and the name lives in both homes, so deleteFile removes only the cached copy while the other copy stays listed and readable (in the order above, with the older content), and close fails (an AssertionError with -ea; with -da, on 9.0.0 and later, a FileAlreadyExistsException, after which the file is in neither home).

bugs.area: store / ByteBuffersDirectory (rename vs. a concurrent createOutput or rename onto the source name)
bugs.title: ByteBuffersDirectory.rename ends with a leftover unconditional files.remove(source), so a file that another thread creates (createOutput) or renames onto the source name while the rename runs is silently deleted, although that thread's call returned normally
bugs.summary: You share one ByteBuffersDirectory between two threads: one renames file 'a' to a new name while the other creates a new 'a' (createOutput, write, close) or renames a temp file onto 'a', and you expect the new 'a' to stay until someone deletes or renames it, as it does on FSDirectory. Instead, now and then the new file vanishes: rename has already moved its own entry with the checked files.remove(source, file) and then runs a leftover unconditional files.remove(source), which can only remove a different entry, the one the other thread has just put under 'a'. Neither call reports an error; afterwards listAll lacks the file and openInput throws NoSuchFileException (stress tests lose between 1 and a few hundred files per 100,000 rounds on every run).

bugs.area: misc / index tools (IndexSplitter.split, SegmentInfos.commit durability)
bugs.title: IndexSplitter.split publishes a durable commit in the destination index without fsyncing the segment files it copied, so an OS crash or power loss soon after a split can leave a destination whose newest commit references empty files and cannot be opened
bugs.summary: You copy segments into a new index with IndexSplitter (new IndexSplitter(src).split(dest, segments), or the command line 'IndexSplitter <src> <dest> <segments>'), and the machine crashes or loses power shortly after the call returns. You expect what every Lucene commit is built for (Directory.sync javadoc: Lucene syncs files 'to prevent a machine/OS crash from corrupting the index'; IndexWriter.commit syncs all referenced files first): the destination's commit only references files whose bytes are on stable storage. Instead split copies the segment files with Files.copy and never fsyncs them, and SegmentInfos.commit then fsyncs only the new segments_N and the directory, so the commit and the copied file names can survive the crash while the copied.si,.cfs and.cfe data does not, and opening the destination fails (CorruptSegmentInfoException on _1.si on main, CorruptIndexException on 10.5.2 and 9.12.3, in the simulated post-crash state).

bugs.area: index / IndexFileDeleter and util/FileDeleter (deletion of expired commits, crash durability)
bugs.title: After a commit, IndexFileDeleter deletes the old segments_N and then the files only it referenced with no directory fsync in between, so an OS crash that persists those unlinks out of order can leave a stale older commit that blocks IndexWriter
bugs.summary: You index with IndexWriter on an FSDirectory with default settings and commit; after the new commit is fsynced, the default deletion policy removes the previous commit, first its segments_N and then the files only it used. You expect that an OS crash or power loss at that point leaves the old commit either complete or gone, which is what the FileDeleter comments and the LUCENE-6616 CHANGES entry ('the index is never left in a state where an expired segments_N references non-existing files') describe. Instead nothing fsyncs the directory between the two deletion passes, so on a file system that persists those unlinks out of order the old segments_N can survive while its _N.si or compound files are gone; DirectoryReader still opens the newest commit, but new IndexWriter fails (CorruptSegmentInfoException on main), listCommits throws and CheckIndex reports corruption (shown in crash states built in software from the real operation sequence; no physical crash was run).

bugs.area: index / deletion policies (PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy persistence, directory fsync)
bugs.title: PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy.snapshot and release return before the new save file's name is durable: persist fsyncs snapshots_N but never calls Directory.syncMetaData, so an OS crash or power loss can lose an acknowledged snapshot
bugs.summary: You protect a commit with PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy.snapshot, whose javadoc says that once the method returns the snapshot information is persisted in the directory. Instead persist writes and fsyncs the new snapshots_N file but never fsyncs the directory (Directory.syncMetaData), the step Lucene's own commit takes because a new file's name is not durable until then. After an OS crash or power loss the save file can be gone: the snapshot count comes back as 0 and, with the snapshots in a separate Directory, the reopened IndexWriter deletes the commit the snapshot was protecting (a lost release instead brings a released snapshot back).

bugs.area: util / automaton
bugs.title: RegExp numeric interval <n-m> accepts a leading '+' on a bound and counts it as a digit, so <+1-+9> matches 01..09 instead of 1..9 and <+100-999> loses its fixed width
bugs.summary: You run a RegexpQuery, or a classic QueryParser query /<+1-+9>/, on a field with the terms 5 and 05. The RegExp javadoc says interval bounds are non-negative decimal integers and that bounds with the same number of digits fix the length of the matching strings, so you expect either an 'interval syntax error' (as for '-1', ' 1' or an overflowing bound) or the meaning of <1-9>, which matches 5. Instead the parser accepts the '+' and counts it as a digit, so <+1-+9> matches only 01 to 09 and returns 05; <+1-9> and <+100-999> lose their fixed width and accept any number of leading zeros, and <+100-+999> means 0100 to 0999.

bugs.area: core / analysis: AutomatonToTokenStream (automaton to token-graph conversion)
bugs.title: AutomatonToTokenStream casts each transition label to char, so a label above U+FFFF becomes a different character (U+10400 comes out as U+0400, U+1F600 as U+F600, U+10000 as a NUL char)
bugs.summary: You build an automaton with Lucene's standard code-point constructors, for example Automata.makeString("\uD801\uDC00") (U+10400) or new RegExp("a" + an emoji).toAutomaton, and convert it with AutomatonToTokenStream.toTokenStream, whose javadoc says the stream releases the automaton's edges as tokens. bugs.area: facet / taxonomy NRT reopen (DirectoryTaxonomyWriter.replaceTaxonomy and deleteAll epoch vs DirectoryTaxonomyReader.doOpenIfChanged)
bugs.title: An NRT DirectoryTaxonomyReader reopened during DirectoryTaxonomyWriter.replaceTaxonomy keeps the replaced taxonomy's ordinal/label caches and parent arrays, because the epoch is incremented only after the content change (wrong labels that persist, or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from openIfChanged)
bugs.summary: You keep a near-real-time taxonomy reader open on a DirectoryTaxonomyWriter and refresh it with openIfChanged while the writer swaps in a rebuilt taxonomy with replaceTaxonomy, for example [a, b] replaced by [b, a]. You expect the refreshed reader to show either the old taxonomy or the new one, each with its own ordinals and labels, as the reader/writer concurrency contract and the reader's own 'was the taxonomy recreated?' check intend. Instead, a refresh that lands after the new content is visible but before replaceTaxonomy increments its epoch is treated as a plain append and reuses the replaced taxonomy's caches and parent arrays: it answers getOrdinal(a)=1 and getPath(1)=a, facet counts over the new index (three b documents, one a) come out labelled 'a (3), b (1)' instead of 'b (3), a (1)', and every later openIfChanged returns null, so the wrong reader stays current until the taxonomy changes again (with a smaller replacement the refresh throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead).

bugs.area: index / IndexWriter construction from a reader's IndexCommit (SegmentInfos.version; DirectoryReader.isCurrent and openIfChanged)
bugs.title: IndexWriter opened from an older reader's IndexCommit takes SegmentInfos.version from that reader, not from the newest commit, so its commits can reuse the version of a newer commit and a reader still open on that commit reports isCurrent=true and openIfChanged returns null
bugs.summary: You keep an older commit (for example with NoDeletionPolicy or a snapshot), open a reader on it, and later go back to it by opening a new IndexWriter with setIndexCommit(thatReader.getIndexCommit) and committing, while another reader is still open on a newer commit. You expect that reader to notice the new commits (isCurrent false, openIfChanged returning the latest commit), as it does when the same commit is taken from DirectoryReader.listCommits. Instead the writer restarts SegmentInfos.version from the old reader instead of from the newest commit, so one of its commits can get exactly the newer commit's version (segments_3 holding [a, b, c] and segments_5 holding [a] are both version 10), and the stale reader reports isCurrent=true, openIfChanged returns null and SearcherLifetimeManager.record throws IllegalArgumentException.

bugs.area: index / IndexWriter addIndexes(CodecReader...) vs rollback (AddIndexesMergeSource, ConcurrentMergeScheduler)
bugs.title: addIndexes(CodecReader...) can register a merge and start a merge thread after a concurrent rollback has returned, because AddIndexesMergeSource.registerMerge does not re-check that merges are enabled
bugs.summary: You call addIndexes(CodecReader...) on one thread while another thread calls rollback on the same writer (or the writer closes itself after a tragic error). You expect that once rollback has returned the writer is closed and starts no more merges, so the addIndexes call just fails; Lucene's own TestAddIndexes rollback tests assert that no merge thread is left. Instead, if rollback lands while addIndexes is asking the merge policy for its merges, the merge is registered after rollback has already aborted all merges, and ConcurrentMergeScheduler starts a new merge thread after rollback and the scheduler's close have returned; that thread throws an uncaught MergeException (AlreadyClosedException 'Lock instance already released' on 10.3.0 and later, 'this IndexWriter is closed' on 9.4.0-10.2.2) and addIndexes throws AlreadyClosedException.

(vigyasharma, merged by mikemccand): it replaced the atomic synchronized { ensureOpen; assert merges.areEnabled; runningAddIndexesMerges.add(merger); } block with an up-front ensureOpen + merges.areEnabled check under the IndexWriter lock, an unlocked MergePolicy.findMerges(CodecReader...) call and AddIndexesMergeSource.registerMerge, which does not check again [read]

bugs.area: index / IndexWriter forceMergeDeletes MergeObserver (MergePolicy.MergeObserver, MergeSpecification.await)
bugs.title: MergeObserver.await and await(timeout) return true after a failed or aborted merge, although their javadoc says they return false on error
bugs.summary: You call IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes(false), which starts the merges in the background and returns a MergeObserver, and then call observer.await to learn whether they worked; its javadoc says it returns true if all merges completed successfully and false on error. Instead it returns true even when the merge failed with an IOException or was aborted by rollback or deleteAll, because every merge's completion future is completed normally with a success flag that await never reads. A caller that trusts the result believes the deleted documents were merged away although the merge never finished.

bugs.area: search / ReferenceManager refresh listeners (ControlledRealTimeReopenThread, LiveFieldValues)
bugs.title: A ReferenceManager refresh that throws is reported to its refresh listeners as afterRefresh(false), the same signal as 'nothing changed', so ControlledRealTimeReopenThread.waitForGeneration returns true for a change the current searcher does not contain and LiveFieldValues drops the values it buffered
bugs.summary: You add, delete or update a document and wait for it with ControlledRealTimeReopenThread.waitForGeneration (or record its value in LiveFieldValues), and the next refresh of the SearcherManager throws, for example because a warm-up query in the SearcherFactory fails or an I/O error hits while the new segment is opened. You expect waitForGeneration to keep waiting or time out, and LiveFieldValues to keep the value, because the old searcher is still current and does not contain the change. Instead ReferenceManager.doMaybeRefresh calls every listener's afterRefresh(false) from a finally block, the same call a refresh that found nothing to do makes, so ControlledRealTimeReopenThread advances its searching generation and wakes the waiters with true, and LiveFieldValues throws away its buffered values.

bugs.area: replicator / NRT segment replication (ReplicaNode.commit commit user data, PrimaryNode.getLastCommitVersion)
bugs.title: An NRT replica's commit can store in VERSION_KEY the version of a newer NRT point installed during its fsync, so the commit claims a version ahead of the SegmentInfos it holds
bugs.summary: You run Lucene's NRT segment replication and call commit on a replica while the primary keeps publishing NRT points, and during the commit's fsync the replica installs a newer point (version 5, documents [d1, d2]). You expect the commit's VERSION_KEY to name the version whose content it holds (version 3, [d1]), or at worst an older one, because the module uses that value as the place to resume replaying operations and PrimaryNode.commit accepts only a lagging value ('replaying more ops than necessary'). Instead commit writes the SegmentInfos it captured before the fsync (version 3) but reads VERSION_KEY from the searcher that is current after it (5), so a primary started on that commit reports getLastCommitVersion=5 while it holds only d1, and a replay from version 5 skips d2.

bugs.area: replicator / NRT segment replication (ReplicaNode.newNRTPoint, maybeNewPrimary, launchPreCopyMerge: primaryGen fencing)
bugs.title: An NRT replica acts on a late notification from an older primary generation: ReplicaNode.maybeNewPrimary deletes the current primary's pre-copied merged segment before its only check, an assert, so the replica's cut-over to the merged point fails or the segment is copied again (with or without assertions), and with assertions off lastPrimaryGen also moves back
bugs.summary: You run Lucene's NRT segment replication and fail over cleanly: the old primary (generation 1) is closed, then replica A is promoted to primary (generation 2), and replica B follows A and pre-copies A's merged segment. A last notification from the old primary, delayed in transit, then reaches B; you expect B to ignore it, as it already ignores out-of-order older NRT versions, because the primary generation only ever grows. Instead ReplicaNode.maybeNewPrimary treats the older generation as a primary change and deletes A's pre-copied merged files before its only check (an assert), so B's cut-over to A's merged point fails with '_3.si cannot be read - it may be missing or corrupt' or B copies the merged segment again, and with assertions off B also sets lastPrimaryGen back to 1.

bugs.area: replicator / NRT segment replication (ReplicaNode.launchPreCopyMerge merge pre-copy, ReplicaNode.newNRTPoint)
bugs.title: An NRT replica's merge pre-copy callback (ReplicaNode.launchPreCopyMerge) synchronizes on itself instead of the ReplicaNode, so a primary change that lands while it installs the merged files leaves the old primary's pre-copied merged files pending and on disk
bugs.summary: You run Lucene's NRT segment replication with merge pre-copy: the primary asks replica B to pre-copy a merged segment, and just as B has copied the bytes and is renaming the files into place, another node is promoted to primary and B receives its first NRT point (primaryGen 2). You expect B either to install the merged files and then discard them in the switch, or to notice the switch and cancel the pre-copy, because newNRTPoint says it discards the old primary's pre-copied merged segments and the callback itself checks whether the primary changed. Instead the callback's synchronized (this) locks the anonymous CopyJob.OnceDone, not the ReplicaNode, so the switch runs in the middle of it and B follows primaryGen 2 with the old primary's merged files [_2.cfe, _2.cfs, _2.si] still in pendingMergeFiles and on disk (with -ea, the new primary's later pre-copy of a same-named merged segment then fails with 'file "_2.si" is already being warmed!').

bugs.area: search / top-k dynamic pruning (BayesianScoreQuery: BayesianScoreScorer#setMinCompetitiveScore)
bugs.title: BayesianScoreQuery raises the minimum competitive score to at least 1e-7 before passing it to its inner query, so default top-k search silently drops the best hits when every competitive calibrated score is below 1e-7
bugs.summary: You run an ordinary top-k search such as searcher.search(query, 10) with a BayesianScoreQuery whose calibrated scores (probabilities) are all below 1e-7, and more than 1,000 documents match. You expect the same top hits as an exhaustive search, because the scores are a monotone transform of the inner BM25 scores and explain reports exactly those scores. Instead, once the collector starts pruning, BayesianScoreQuery rounds the requested minimum score up to 1e-7 before turning it into a BM25 threshold for the inner query, so the inner query skips documents that are still competitive and the search returns weaker hits (in the repros, in effect the first matches in doc-id order) with no error.

bugs.area: search / top-k dynamic pruning (BayesianScoreQuery: BayesianScoreScorer#setMinCompetitiveScore)
bugs.title: BayesianScoreQuery turns the minimum competitive probability into an inner-score threshold that lies inside the range of inner scores with exactly that probability, so default top-k search can skip a hit that is still competitive
bugs.summary: You run an ordinary top-k search such as searcher.search(query, 10) with a BayesianScoreQuery, and more than 1,000 documents match. You expect the same top hits as an exhaustive search, because the probability is a monotone function of the inner score and pruning may skip only documents that score below the current k-th hit. Instead, when a later document's probability is exactly one float step above the k-th hit's (most often when probabilities are close to 1), BayesianScoreQuery turns that probability back into an inner-score threshold with a closed-form inverse that lands in the middle of the range of inner scores that all round to that probability, so the inner query skips the document and the search silently returns the weaker hit.

bugs.area: search / top-k dynamic pruning (block-max conjunction and MaxScore bulk scorers)
bugs.title: ScorerUtil.minRequiredScore returns NaN when the minimum competitive score is +Infinity, so block-max conjunctions and MaxScore disjunctions drop documents that score +Infinity
bugs.summary: You run an ordinary top-k search, for example IndexSearcher#search(query, 1), with a two-clause conjunction or disjunction whose scores can overflow to +Infinity (two FeatureField linear queries over very large feature values, or two clauses with very large finite boosts). You expect the best documents first, +Infinity before Float.MAX_VALUE and ties by ascending doc id, as Lucene 10.2.2 returns them. Instead, once the minimum competitive score reaches +Infinity, ScorerUtil.minRequiredScore returns NaN and filterCompetitiveHits discards every remaining candidate, so the search silently returns doc 0 scoring Float.MAX_VALUE instead of doc 3000 scoring +Infinity (one thread, one segment), or docs 100, 101, 102 instead of the equally scored docs 0, 1, 2 (a concurrent search in which the slice with the higher doc ids finishes first).

bugs.area: search / top-k dynamic pruning (WANDScorer)
bugs.title: WANDScorer mishandles a minimum competitive score of +Infinity: an assertion fails with -ea, and with -da it prunes documents that score +Infinity
bugs.summary: You run a top-k search whose top-level disjunction runs on WANDScorer, for example three FeatureField linear SHOULD clauses with minimumNumberShouldMatch 2, over documents whose finite clause scores add up past Float.MAX_VALUE, so that they score +Infinity. You expect the same documents as an exhaustive (COMPLETE) search: hits tied at +Infinity stay competitive and are ordered by doc id (or by the next sort field). Instead, once the collector raises the minimum competitive score to +Infinity, WANDScorer.scaleMinScore fails its 'Float.isFinite(minScore)' assertion with -ea (even in a single-threaded search), and with -da it saturates the bound to Long.MAX_VALUE and prunes every remaining document, so a concurrent search with the default slicing returns docs 23, 24, 25 instead of 0, 1, 2, all scoring +Infinity.
bugs.introduced_commit: 4fc5a872ded (LUCENE-4100 'Faster disjunctions when the hit count is not needed', a JIRA patch committed directly, no GitHub PR) created WANDScorer and scaleMinScore with only a not-NaN assertion and a saturating cast ('cast might lower the value again if scaled > Long.MAX_VALUE, which is fine'), which turns a +Infinity minimum into Long.MAX_VALUE and rejects every document: the -da wrong results [read]; d9e37f31230 (main; branch_9x db0e712cad3), apache/lucene#794 'Improve accuracy of scaled scores in WANDScorer' (LUCENE-10503; the commit message says LUCENE-10153 by mistake), tightened the assertion to Float.isFinite(minScore): the -ea AssertionError [exec]; the stock collectors reach the -da form through 947f82679af (LUCENE-8507: TopFieldCollector passes the raw bottom score for a score-first sort, 8.0.0) and LUCENE-8992 (apache/lucene-solr#904, branch_8x 1c23a3c14e7: the cross-slice shared bound passes the raw global score to leaves with smaller doc ids, 8.4.0) [exec]; commits located with git log -S and the tag history in the history clone [read]; a long-standing bug, not a recent regression

bugs.area: core / search and document: query parameter validation (DisjunctionMaxQuery, LatLonPoint distance feature query)
bugs.title: DisjunctionMaxQuery and LatLonPoint.newDistanceFeatureQuery accept a NaN tie-breaker or pivot distance (the pivot also +Infinity) because their range checks are false for NaN, so hits score NaN and a NaN query is not equal to itself
bugs.summary: You build a DisjunctionMaxQuery with tieBreakerMultiplier NaN (for example a computed value, or the XML query parser text tieBreaker='NaN'), or a LatLonPoint.newDistanceFeatureQuery with pivotDistance NaN or +Infinity, and expect the IllegalArgumentException that both constructors already throw for every other out-of-range value ('tieBreakerMultiplier must be in [0, 1]', 'pivotDistance must be > 0'). Instead the value is accepted, because the checks are written as 'x < 0 || x > 1' and 'x <= 0', which are false for NaN (and '<= 0' is false for +Infinity): on main the hits come back with NaN scores, although the distance feature javadoc promises scores in [0, weight], and for a NaN value q.equals(q) is false because equals compares the field with ==. Older releases are worse: with a NaN tie-breaker, 8.0.0 and 8.11.4 return no top-k hits while count finds them, and 9.12.3 with assertions off returns a sentinel ScoreDoc (doc 2147483647, score -Infinity) in place of a hit.
bugs.introduced_commit: Two sites, both first released in 8.0.0 [read]. (1) DisjunctionMaxQuery: e3f90385b492 'LUCENE-8097: Implement maxScore on disjunctions.' (jpountz; JIRA patch, no GitHub PR; issue now apache/lucene#9145) added 'if (tieBreakerMultiplier < 0 || tieBreakerMultiplier > 1) throw IAE' to the DisjunctionMaxQuery constructor and the same check to the package-private DisjunctionMaxScorer constructor. Not a regression in the usual sense: before it the class had no validation at all, and equals has compared the float with == since the class was added (3c10854e00f, LUCENE-323, 2005, Lucene 1.9) [exec]. (2) LatLonPointDistanceFeatureQuery: 10060a6237cc 'LUCENE-8482: Added feature query in LatLonPoint to boost results by distance' (iverase; JIRA patch; issue now apache/lucene#9528) created the class with 'if (pivotDistance <= 0) throw IAE' and the == equals, together with LatLonPoint.newDistanceFeatureQuery; the check was copied from the long-valued recency feature query (LUCENE-8340), where NaN cannot occur. Neither issue discusses NaN.

bugs.area: core / document: XY distance sort (XYDocValuesField.newDistanceSort, XYPointSortField, XYPointDistanceComparator)
bugs.title: XYDocValuesField.newDistanceSort accepts a NaN or infinite origin although its javadoc promises IllegalArgumentException for invalid coordinates (the LatLon twin and every other XY entry point reject such values); with a NaN origin, documents without a location sort first instead of last
bugs.summary: You build a distance sort with XYDocValuesField.newDistanceSort("p", Float.NaN, 0f), or with an infinite x or y, and expect the IllegalArgumentException that its javadoc promises when the 'location has invalid coordinates', as LatLonDocValuesField.newDistanceSort throws for NaN and as the XYDocValuesField constructor, XYPointField.newDistanceQuery and XYCircle throw for the same values. Instead the sort is built and the search runs, because the XYPointSortField constructor checks only that the field name is not null. With a NaN origin every distance is NaN, which Double.compare orders after +Infinity, so a document without a location (distance +Infinity, documented as 'missing values sort last') is returned before the documents that have one; with an infinite origin all distances tie at +Infinity.

bugs.area: queries / function
bugs.title: FunctionRangeQuery over Int/Long/EnumFieldSource turns an exclusive bound at the type limit into an inclusive one
bugs.summary: You run a FunctionRangeQuery over an IntFieldSource, LongFieldSource or EnumFieldSource with an exclusive bound exactly at the type limit, such as n > Integer.MAX_VALUE. You expect no document to match. Instead getRangeScorer adjusts an exclusive bound only when it is not already at the limit (if (!includeLower && lower < Integer.MAX_VALUE) lower++), so at the limit the bound stays inclusive and the document whose value is exactly MAX (or MIN) matches: 1 hit instead of 0.

bugs.area: core store + index / stored string fields (DataInput.readString decode, IndexWriter.MAX_STORED_STRING_LENGTH check)
bugs.title: IndexWriter accepts a stored string of 2^30 - 1 or more UTF-8 bytes of non-Latin-1 text (from about half of its own MAX_STORED_STRING_LENGTH up), but DataInput.readString can never decode it, so StoredFields#document, visitor-path merges and index-sorted flushes throw OutOfMemoryError
bugs.summary: You store a text field of 357,913,941 CJK characters (1,073,741,823 UTF-8 bytes, about half of what IndexWriter's own length check, MAX_STORED_STRING_LENGTH, allows) with the default codec, and IndexWriter accepts and commits it. You expect StoredFields#document to return it, as it does for a string one character shorter. Instead every read throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError 'UTF16 String size is 1073741823, should be less than 1073741823', whatever the heap, because DataInput.readString decodes with new String(bytes, 0, length, UTF_8), which on JDK 9 and later sizes its UTF-16 buffer by the byte count and refuses 2^30 - 1 or more units; merges that copy the document through a visitor, and flushes of an index-sorted writer, throw the same Error and close IndexWriter.
bugs.introduced_commit: none bisectable: no release executed on JDK 25 passes (5.5.5 to main) [exec]. Three ingredients [read]: (1) stored strings are decoded with the JDK String(byte,..., UTF-8) constructor since 8af3598b74d (LUCENE-510, first released 2.4.0); the decode site moved with LUCENE-5989 (fd23211957a / 249d0d25fec, 5.2.0) and LUCENE-8805 (5a694ea26ff, 9.0.0, into DataInput.readString), keeping the same constructor; (2) JDK 9 compact strings size the UTF-16 buffer of a non-Latin-1 result by the UTF-8 byte count and refuse about 2^30 or more units (OpenJDK source reading; JDK 8 decodes into a char with no such cap); (3) the documented limit IndexWriter.MAX_STORED_STRING_LENGTH and its IndexWriter check, 2902727a157 (master) / be47009ce76 (branch_6x), LUCENE-7538 (#8589), first released 6.4.0, which states the contract but did not introduce the failure (6.3.0, without the limit, fails identically [exec])

bugs.area: util / BKD points (BKDWriter in-heap sort buffer sizing: HeapPointWriter and the BKDRadixSelector heap writers, reached through Lucene90PointsWriter's public maxMBSortInHeap constructor)
bugs.title: BKDWriter does not cap its in-heap point buffer at the Java array limit, so with maxMBSortInHeap >= 2048 MB a points merge of more than 2^31 bytes throws NegativeArraySizeException and closes the IndexWriter
bugs.summary: You give a points format a sort budget of 2048 MB or more, for example new Lucene90PointsWriter(state, 512, 2200.0) in a custom codec, and merge segments that hold more than 2 GiB of points of one multi-dimensional field (in the repro 8.4M points of 16 dims x 16 bytes). You expect the merge to succeed, because BKDWriter 'uses up to the specified maxMBSortInHeap heap space for writing', spills to disk beyond it, and its constructor accepts the value. Instead BKDWriter sizes its in-heap buffer as budget / bytesPerDoc points with no cap at the Java array limit, HeapPointWriter computes bytesPerDoc * size in int, the length wraps negative, and forceMerge(1) throws NegativeArraySizeException (-2110967296) and leaves the IndexWriter closed with that tragic exception.

bugs.area: index / IndexingChain aborting-exception classification x util / UTF-16 to UTF-8 sizing (CharTermAttributeImpl.getBytesRef, BytesRefBuilder.copyChars, UnicodeUtil.maxUTF8Length)
bugs.title: A single indexed token of 715,827,878 or more UTF-16 units closes IndexWriter and drops uncommitted documents instead of being rejected as an immense term
bugs.summary: You index a document whose untokenized indexed field (or a TextField analyzed with KeywordAnalyzer) holds one value of 715,827,878 or more characters, for example 'a' repeated 715,827,883 times. You expect what Lucene does for any over-long term: addDocument throws the documented 'immense term' IllegalArgumentException, skips that document and keeps the IndexWriter open with the other buffered documents. Instead the UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion sizes its buffer at 3 bytes per character before the length check, that size overflows int (ArithmeticException) or exceeds the maximum array length (IllegalArgumentException), and because the conversion runs inside the indexing chain's aborting try, IndexWriter closes itself and rolls back every document added since the last commit.

Writer-closing form (the title): LUCENE-5987 (now GitHub #7049) by GitHub mikemccand, c064aaa4850 (branch_5x) / de4c6513bcb (trunk), which made every aborting exception close IndexWriter [read]. Later milestones: LUCENE-6133 (52b13f1946b / d249f8bc337) moved the threshold from about 536.9M to 715,827,878 units; LUCENE-7538 (#8589; be47009ce76 / 2902727a157) made n >= 715,827,883 throw ArithmeticException and added a pre-check for stored fields only

bugs.area: index / in-RAM postings byte slices (ByteSliceReader, TermsHashPerField)
bugs.title: ByteSliceReader's final-slice test (nextIndex + newSize >= endIndex) overflows int when a postings stream's last slice ends exactly at the 2^31-byte end of the in-RAM byte pool, so IndexWriter silently commits up to 3 wrong postings bytes that CheckIndex accepts
bugs.summary: You add one very large document whose postings fill the indexing thread's in-RAM byte pool to its very last byte (global offset 2^31), and you expect the flushed segment to hold exactly the positions and payloads you indexed, or a loud failure such as the ArithmeticException Lucene has thrown since 9.8.0 once the pool would grow further. Instead, if one term's postings stream ends in the slice that occupies the pool's last bytes, ByteSliceReader.nextSlice computes nextIndex + newSize = 2^31 in int, which wraps negative, so it treats that final slice as non-final, reads its last 3 data bytes plus the level marker as a forwarding address, and returns the stream's last 1-3 bytes from an unrelated part of the pool. IndexWriter commits with no exception (with -ea and -da) and CheckIndex reports the segment clean; in the executed run the last 3 bytes of a 355-byte payload, 0x41 0x42 0x43, read back as 0x11.
bugs.introduced_commit: cff5767e443411c78b199fbf9686d1ec672e38f0 (svn r553236, LUCENE-843 'speed up IndexWriter performance', JIRA era, no GitHub PR; committed by mikemccand): it added DocumentsWriter with a nested ByteSliceReader whose 'if (nextIndex + newSize >= endIndex)' (DocumentsWriter.java:2432) and 'if (startIndex+firstSize >= endIndex)' (:2385) are the two lines on main today (ByteSliceReader.java:109 and:58); moved unchanged to its own file by e5f9b4e1cb3 (LUCENE-1212, 2008-03-12) [read]. Latent since then, not a regression: #12392 (b88d3e19889, 2023-06-28, the pool's 2^31 cap) neither caused nor fixed it (9.7.0 and 9.8.0 both fail) [exec]

bugs.area: search / HNSW (merge-time graph reuse: old-to-new ordinal mapping in IncrementalHnswGraphMerger and ConcurrentHnswMerger)
bugs.title: HNSW merge with graph reuse throws BufferAllocationException when the reused graph has more than 805,306,368 vectors
bugs.summary: You merge an HNSW vector field in which one segment's graph has more than 805,306,368 vectors (Lucene writes such a segment without error, for example by merging smaller graphs) and expect the merge to reuse that graph as it does at any smaller size, because no HNSW vector-count limit is documented or enforced below IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS. Instead both mergers presize an IntIntHashMap to the graph size to map old to new ordinals, and that map's fixed 0.75 load factor and 2^30-slot table cap make its constructor throw BufferAllocationException ('Maximum array size exceeded for this load factor') before any other work. The merge fails again on every retry, so such a segment can never be merged with graph reuse; by code reading the IndexWriter is also closed as a tragic event.

bugs.area: facet / DrillSideways (sequential DrillSidewaysScorer, union and drill-down-advance strategies)
bugs.title: Sequential DrillSideways never returns on a segment of more than 2^31 - 2048 documents: DrillSidewaysScorer's int chunk start wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, so its union and drill-down-advance loops never exit (released since 4.2.0)
bugs.summary: You run a faceted DrillSideways search in the default sequential mode on an index whose single segment holds more than 2,147,481,600 documents, which IndexWriter accepts (MAX_DOCS = 2,147,483,519), and expect it to return its hits as it does on a segment 2,048 documents smaller. Instead DrillSidewaysScorer's union and drill-down-advance loops walk the segment in 2048-document chunks with an int nextChunkStart that wraps from 2^31 - 2048 to Integer.MIN_VALUE before the exit test 'nextChunkStart >= maxDoc' can fire, so the search thread spins forever and the hits of the last chunk are never collected. Through the public API on a real segment of MAX_DOCS documents the stock search did not return within 300 s, while the fixed build returned its 3 hits in 0.033 s.

It added DrillSidewaysScorer with CHUNK = 2048, 'int nextChunkStart = CHUNK' and, in doDrillDownAdvanceScoring and doUnionScoring, 'if (nextChunkStart >= maxDoc) break;' followed by 'nextChunkStart += CHUNK;' (2 sites per method) [read] [exec]

bugs.area: search / BooleanQuery MUST_NOT bulk scoring (ReqExclBulkScorer)
bugs.title: ReqExclBulkScorer.WindowBits.applyMask adds offset + bitSet.length in int, so FILTER/MUST + MUST_NOT queries silently drop every match in a 4096-doc window based at doc 2^31-4096 or above (up to the last 3,967 doc IDs of a segment near IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS)
bugs.summary: You index one segment of IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS (2,147,483,519) documents with default settings, one of which has b:y, and count the matches of +*:* -b:y (MatchAllDocsQuery as FILTER plus a MUST_NOT term query) with a plain IndexSearcher; you expect 2,147,483,518. Instead you get 2,147,479,551: all 3,967 documents of the last window [2,147,479,552, MAX_DOCS) are silently missing, because ReqExclBulkScorer's WindowBits.applyMask computes Math.min(NO_MORE_DOCS, offset + bitSet.length) in int, the sum wraps negative for a 4096-bit window based at 2^31-4096 or above, and the method then clears the whole window. Only segments with more than 2,147,479,552 documents and required clauses denser than 0.3% of maxDoc are affected, and only unreleased code (main and the 10.x / 10.6 branches since #16669) has the bug.

bugs.area: codecs / postings reader (Lucene104 BlockPostingsEnum position bookkeeping; also the Lucene101, Lucene103, Lucene99 and Lucene90 readers in backward-codecs)
bugs.title: Postings readers count skipped positions in an int, so once the skipped occurrences of one term within a postings block pass Integer.MAX_VALUE, nextPosition returns an earlier document's positions and phrase queries silently miss matches
bugs.summary: You index documents that each stay within Lucene's per-document limits but repeat one term about a billion times and run PhraseQuery f:"v t", which only C matches. You expect the postings reader to return C's own positions (101, 102, 103,...) and the query to find C. Instead the reader adds up the frequencies of the documents whose positions it skipped in an int, the sum 2,147,483,696 wraps negative, the skip is not done, and nextPosition returns the first skipped document's positions (1, 2, 3), so the query finds 0 hits with assertions off (with assertions on, an internal assertion fails instead).

bugs.area: misc / similarities (SweetSpotSimilarity lengthNorm; NaN effect on impacts-based top-k pruning in core search)
bugs.title: SweetSpotSimilarity.lengthNorm adds abs(x-min) + abs(x-max) in int, so a field of 1,073,741,848 or more terms (reachable with one custom term frequency) gets a NaN norm: the document is never collected, and default top-k search also skips competitive documents in the same postings block and skip range
bugs.summary: You score with SweetSpotSimilarity (default factors) and index one document whose DOCS_AND_FREQS field has a length of at least 1,073,741,848, for example one token with custom term frequency 1.1e9 or about 1.07e9 ordinary tokens, expecting the documented lengthNorm 1/sqrt(x) (about 3.05e-5, the ClassicSimilarity value) and an ordinary, low-ranked hit. Instead lengthNorm's int sum |x-1| + |x-1| wraps negative, so the norm and the score are NaN and the document is never collected (exhaustive collection returns 5,999 of 6,000 matches); because the NaN also makes the postings block's maximum score NaN, default top-k search skips that block and the skip range above it, so search(q, 7) on a 10,000-document index misses three documents that score 1.0 and returns documents that score 0.5 instead. ClassicSimilarity on the same index is correct.

bugs.area: suggest / FreeTextSuggester (n-gram counts stored as long FST outputs; lookup-side decode)
bugs.title: FreeTextSuggester.decodeWeight casts n-gram counts to int, so a word or context seen more than Integer.MAX_VALUE times gets a negative or wrapped count: lookup returns scores outside the documented 0.0 to 1.0 range and can rank the most frequent word last
bugs.summary: You build a FreeTextSuggester from text in which one word occurs more than Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647) times and expect lookup to rank that word first with a score near 1.0, because the class javadoc says each result value is Long.MAX_VALUE times a score from 0.0 to 1.0 and build counts n-grams as long. Instead decodeWeight returns (int) (Long.MAX_VALUE - output), so a count of 2,148,532,224 comes back as -2,146,435,072 and lookup('a', 2) returns [ab score 0.0, a score -0.999]: a negative score, with the most frequent word ranked below a word seen once. The same cast decodes context counts, so every prediction from a context seen that often is scored wrongly, and counts above 2^32 wrap to small positive numbers that stay inside the 0..1 range and are silently wrong.
bugs.introduced_commit: b50a2edbb2389797a7354775414052df91b108f6 (trunk, svn r1528517, 'LUCENE-5214: add FreeTextSuggester', Michael McCandless (@mikemccand), 2013-10-02) and its same-day branch_4x backport 9494be7ec2ae84e88b6fc07046c35cac15e790d2 (svn r1528521), the commit contained in 4.6.0; issue LUCENE-5214 = apache/lucene#6278, no pull request (Subversion era). Not a regression: the cast 'return (int)(Long.MAX_VALUE - output);' is in the first version of the class [read]; the only later touch, 2cbf261032d (LUCENE-9570, 2021-01-05), changed whitespace only. The same first commit already counts (totTokens, totalTermFreq), encodes (encodeWeight(long) = Long.MAX_VALUE - count, no range check) and stores (writeVLong) counts as long, and decodeWeight is declared to return long. Probable origin [inference from code, not stated anywhere]: the int-weight decoder of the sibling suggesters (WFSTCompletionLookup and AnalyzingSuggester at the parent commit return (int)(Integer.MAX_VALUE - encoded) and reject weights above Integer.MAX_VALUE at encode time).

bugs.area: store / ByteBuffersDataOutput
bugs.title: ByteBuffersDataOutput.copyBytes narrows its long length to a signed int, so a copy of 2 GiB or more (for example Directory.copyFrom into a ByteBuffersDirectory) silently copies nothing or only (int) numBytes bytes
bugs.summary: You copy 2 GiB or more into an in-heap ByteBuffersDataOutput, for example with Directory.copyFrom or IndexWriter.addIndexes(Directory) into a ByteBuffersDirectory. You expect every byte to be copied, as DataOutput.copyBytes(DataInput, long numBytes) promises ('Copy numBytes bytes from input to ourself') and as Lucene 9.2.0 does. Instead the override stores the length in an int, copies max(0, (int) numBytes) bytes (nothing at all for any length from 2^31 to 2^32-1) and returns normally, so the destination file is empty or truncated with no exception; a copied index then fails to open with CorruptIndexException.

bugs.area: codecs / stored fields (Lucene90 compressing writer)
bugs.title: Stored fields writer: the int slice loop in flush wraps once a chunk is larger than 2,147,450,880 bytes, so a ~2 GiB document within the documented per-document limit closes IndexWriter when smaller documents are still buffered in its chunk
bugs.summary: You index a small document and then, before the chunk fills, one document with about 2 GiB of stored content that is within the documented per-document limit, for example exactly 2^31 - 81,920 = 2,147,401,728 serialized bytes after a 49,153-byte document. You expect both to be indexed, as they are when the first document is one byte smaller. Instead flush steps through the chunk with an int offset that wraps past Integer.MAX_VALUE, ByteBuffersDataInput.slice rejects the negative offset with IllegalArgumentException, and IndexWriter closes itself and drops every uncommitted document.

bugs.area: codecs / stored fields (Lucene90StoredFieldsFormat javadoc vs Lucene90CompressingStoredFieldsFormat)
bugs.title: Lucene90StoredFieldsFormat (the default codec's stored fields) documents a per-document limit of 2^31 - 2^14 bytes, but the format it delegates to documents and enforces 2^31 - chunkSize (chunks of 81,920 / 491,520 bytes), so a document just below the stated limit can fail with ArithmeticException and close IndexWriter (documentation defect: the javadoc value has been stale since the chunks grew past 16 KiB)
bugs.summary: You read the default codec's stored-fields documentation (Lucene90StoredFieldsFormat, 'Known limitations'), which says only individual documents larger than 2^31 - 2^14 = 2,147,467,264 bytes are unsupported, and you index a document of 2,147,403,644 serialized bytes, below that limit, right after a small document. addDocument fails with ArithmeticException ('integer overflow') and IndexWriter closes itself, while the same big document on its own is indexed. The writer does what the class it delegates to, Lucene90CompressingStoredFieldsFormat, documents (at most 2^31 - chunkSize bytes, with chunks of 81,920 or 491,520 bytes today); the outer javadoc's number was right only when chunks were 16 KiB and was never updated.

bugs.title: addIndexes(CodecReader...) with the default config rejects inputs whose maxDoc sum, deleted documents included, exceeds MAX_DOCS although only their live documents are added, because it always builds a merged view of the inputs for OneMerge#reorder (regression since 9.9.0)
bugs.summary: You call IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) with readers that have many deleted or filtered-out documents, so their live documents fit under IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS but their maxDoc values (deleted documents included) add up to more. You expect the call to succeed, since addIndexes counts and reserves only live documents, its javadoc throws IllegalArgumentException only if the index would exceed MAX_DOCS, and 9.8.0 accepted the same call. Instead, with the default configuration it throws IllegalArgumentException 'Too many documents: composite IndexReaders cannot exceed...' and adds nothing, because since 9.9.0 addIndexesReaderMerge always wraps the inputs in a SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper (a MultiReader over the uncompacted inputs) for OneMerge#reorder, whose default returns null and discards the view.

bugs.area: misc / index tools (MultiPassIndexSplitter.split, round-robin mode)
bugs.title: MultiPassIndexSplitter's round-robin split loses or duplicates the last few documents of an index at about IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS for most part counts of 145 or more, because its int test (j + numParts - i) % numParts overflows
bugs.summary: You split an index of IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS (2,147,483,519) documents with MultiPassIndexSplitter in round-robin mode, the command-line default, into 145 parts, and expect every document in exactly one part (part i gets the documents whose id j has j % numParts == i), as the split javadoc says: ids are 'assigned in a deterministic round-robin fashion to one of the output splits'. Instead the parts hold 2,147,483,527 documents in total: documents 2,147,483,511..518 belong to parts 16..23 but are also copied into parts 0..7, and with 149 parts documents 2,147,483,509..518 end up in no part at all; nothing reports an error. The cause is the keep test (j + numParts - i) % numParts == 0 at MultiPassIndexSplitter.java:103, computed in int: for the top doc ids j + numParts - i wraps negative and Java's % keeps the sign, while the equivalent j % numParts == i cannot overflow.

bugs.area: util / VectorUtil byte DOT_PRODUCT score x internal/vectorization / Panama MemorySegment byte scorers
bugs.title: Byte DOT_PRODUCT scores (VectorUtil.dotProductScore and the two Panama byte scorers) compute len * 2^15 in int, so from 65,536 dimensions every score is mirrored around 0.5 (closer vectors score lower) and at 131,072 dimensions scores become +/-Infinity or NaN
bugs.summary: You score two byte vectors of 65,536 dimensions with VectorSimilarityFunction.DOT_PRODUCT (or VectorUtil.dotProductScore, or run a KnnByteVectorQuery on a byte DOT_PRODUCT field indexed through a format that raises getMaxDimensions) and expect the documented score 0.5 + dot / (len * 2^15): within [0, 1] and higher for more similar vectors. Instead the divisor len * (1 << 15) is multiplied in int before the cast to float, so from 65,536 dimensions it wraps to a negative number and every score is mirrored around 0.5: a vector identical to an all-ones query scores 0.49996948 and its opposite 0.5000305, and kNN returns the documents in exactly reverse order. At 131,072 dimensions the divisor wraps to 0 and the scores are +Infinity, -Infinity or NaN.

bugs.area: core vectorization + misc native C / opt-in native int8 dot product (NativeVectorUtilSupport, lucene/misc/src/c/dotProduct.c vdot8s_sve)
bugs.title: The example native int8 dot product (lucene/misc/src/c/dotProduct.c, opt-in via -Dlucene.useNativeDotProduct=true) keeps its SVE loop index in int32, so VectorUtil.dotProduct(byte, byte) on two arrays of at least 2^31 - 4*VL elements (2,147,483,520 at 256-bit SVE, 2,147,483,584 at 128-bit SVE) overflows the loop bound, reads past the end of both arrays and kills the JVM with SIGSEGV in vdot8s_sve
bugs.summary: You enable Lucene's opt-in native dot product (-Dlucene.useNativeDotProduct=true plus a library built from the example lucene/misc/src/c/dotProduct.c) on an SVE machine and call VectorUtil.dotProduct(byte, byte) on two legal arrays of 2,147,483,645 bytes whose exact dot product is 3, expecting 3 as the Panama and default providers return. Instead the SVE kernel vdot8s_sve keeps its loop index and vector length in int32_t, so its loop test 'i + 4 * vec_length <= limit' (dotProduct.c:66) overflows once i reaches 2^31 - 4*VL (VL = SVE vector length in bytes); in the compiled code the bound wraps negative while the load offset is a 64-bit register, so the loop keeps loading past the end of both arrays until it hits an unmapped page and the JVM dies with SIGSEGV in vdot8s_sve. Every length from 2^31 - 4*VL up to the JVM maximum crashes (2,147,483,520 at 256-bit SVE, 2,147,483,584 at 128-bit SVE), while one element less returns the exact result; a 64-bit loop index with svwhilelt_b8_s64 fixes it.

bugs.area: search / HNSW (merge-time graph reuse: IncrementalHnswGraphMerger base-graph selection)
bugs.title: HNSW merge computes a graph's deleted percentage in int, so a graph with more than 21,474,836 deleted vectors (41-100% deleted) passes the 40% DELETE_PCT_THRESHOLD and is reused as the merge base; on main before #16794 the opt-in concurrent merger then threw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for an all-deleted base
bugs.summary: You merge an HNSW vector segment that has had most of its vectors deleted and expect Lucene to rebuild the graph or reuse a cleaner one, because the DELETE_PCT_THRESHOLD javadoc says a graph with more than 40% of its vectors deleted is never selected as the merge base. Once more than 21,474,836 vectors of one graph are deleted, the percentage ((graphSize - live) * 100) / graphSize overflows int and goes negative (-59 for 25M deleted out of 30M), so the guard passes and a graph that is up to 100% deleted becomes the base, in either reader order and also when the segment is merged alone. The default merger still finishes, pruning and repairing the reused graph. On main before #16794 (for example ea57360912ed) the opt-in concurrent merger threw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for an all-deleted base; since #16794 (a9779ef3c193) it rebuilds the graph, and only the wrong choice of merge base remains.

bugs.area: index / IndexWriter flush-control RAM accounting (DocumentsWriterFlushControl.markForFullFlush drops a 0-document DocumentsWriterPerThread; reached through updateDocuments and softUpdateDocuments with an empty block)
bugs.title: IndexWriter.updateDocuments / softUpdateDocuments with an empty block leave about 33 KB of phantom RAM accounting at every refresh or commit that drops the empty per-thread writer, so ramBytesUsed grows without bound and, once it passes the RAM buffer, every later document is flushed into its own segment
bugs.summary: You call IndexWriter.updateDocuments(term, List.of), or softUpdateDocuments(term, List.of, softField), to delete a key's documents and add nothing, then refresh or commit; you expect the delete to apply and nothing to stay buffered, so ramBytesUsed returns to 0 as it does after deleteDocuments(term) or addDocuments(List.of). Instead the call took a per-thread writer and charged its delete buffer (about 33 KB) to the flush control, and the next full flush throws that 0-document writer away without taking the charge back, so ramBytesUsed climbs by about 33 KB per round and never comes down (20 rounds with a default config: 660,800 B). Once the phantom total passes the RAM buffer (about 510 rounds at the default 16 MB) the writer flushes after every document, so 200 small documents become 200 segments; with assertions enabled the writer closes itself with an AssertionError instead.

bugs.title: Merge-on-refresh never releases the file references of a merged segment that is dropped because all its documents were deleted during the merge, so IndexWriter leaves that segment's files on disk until the next writer opens the index

bugs.area: index / merge policy (LogMergePolicy forced-deletes selection, IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes)
bugs.title: LogMergePolicy.findForcedDeletesMerges does not skip segments that are already merging, so IndexWriter rejects the whole run and forceMergeDeletes(true) returns with deletes left in segments that were never merging
bugs.summary: You use LogDocMergePolicy or LogByteSizeMergePolicy and call IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes(true) while another merge is pending or running, for example the natural merge that the call's own flush starts. bugs.area: expressions / SimpleBindings binding resolution (add(String, Expression), getDoubleValuesSource) and the ExpressionValueSource constructor
bugs.title: SimpleBindings rebuilds an Expression binding on every reference, so building the source of bindings that share sub-expressions creates one ExpressionValueSource per path (exponential in the depth of sharing)
bugs.summary: You bind named expressions that use each other with SimpleBindings.add(String, Expression), which the class javadoc documents ('This can be used to reference expressions from other expressions'), and some of them share a sub-expression, for example X1 = L0 + R0 with L0 = X0 + 1 and R0 = X0 * 2, repeated in a chain. You expect getDoubleValuesSource to build each binding a bounded number of times, as building the same graph eagerly with add(String, DoubleValuesSource) does. Instead every reference re-applies expression::getDoubleValuesSource, so the shared graph is expanded into a tree with one ExpressionValueSource per path: 3*(2^d - 1) objects for a chain of d diamonds (196,605 for 49 bindings), and building the source of 70 or more such bindings exhausts a 1 GB heap before any document is read, while the computed values stay correct.

bugs.area: expressions / SimpleBindings.validate (cycle and missing-reference check, CycleDetectionBindings)
bugs.title: SimpleBindings.validate copies the whole binding path into a new set at every step and re-checks every binding once per origin, so validating a plain chain of 2000 expression bindings takes about 45 s instead of about 100 ms (cubic since 8.6.0, a regression from LUCENE-9338)
bugs.summary: You build a chain of named expressions with SimpleBindings.add(String, Expression), each using the previous one (x1 = x0 + 1, x2 = x1 + 1,..., x2000 = x1999 + 1), and call bindings.validate, whose javadoc says it 'Traverses the graph of bindings, checking there are no cycles or missing references'. You expect a graph check that costs about as much as resolving every binding once, as on 8.5.2, where validate of these 2000 bindings took about 100 ms. Instead, since 8.6.0 validate starts a fresh walk from every binding, re-walks everything below it, and copies the whole current path into a new LinkedHashSet at every step, so its cost grows with the cube of the chain length: about 45 s for 2000 bindings and about 575 s for 4000 (at 1000 bindings it allocates 389.9 times the bytes of resolving every binding once), although the answer is still correct.

bugs.area: store / MMapDirectory read advice (MemorySegmentIndexInput slices, compound files)
bugs.title: MMapDirectory applies a slice's read advice to the wrong bytes when the slice starts inside an mmap chunk and crosses into the next one (the #14109 prefetch fix missed this caller of advise)
bugs.summary: You take a slice of an MMapDirectory file with IndexInput#slice(name, offset, length, IOContext) and a context that asks for RANDOM or SEQUENTIAL read advice, as the compound-file reader does for each inner file, and you expect the madvise hint to land on the slice's own pages. When the slice starts inside an mmap chunk and crosses into the next chunk, the hint is applied from the start of that chunk instead: in the repro, a slice of [512 KiB, 1.5 MiB) with 1 MiB chunks puts the RANDOM hint on [0, 1 MiB), so other inner files of a compound file get it, and a short slice that straddles a chunk boundary can get none of its own pages advised. bugs.area: codecs / bloom (BloomFilteringPostingsFormat, DefaultBloomFilterFactory, FuzzySet sizing)
bugs.title: BloomFilteringPostingsFormat's default filter silently stops filtering for segments of 226,279,579 docs or more: FuzzySet.createOptimalSet computes 2 * setSize in int, which wraps negative and yields a 64-bit filter with zero hash functions that answers MAYBE for every key (released since 9.6.0)
bugs.summary: You index a primary key into a field that uses BloomFilteringPostingsFormat with the default filter factory, whose javadoc promises a filter targeting about 10% false positives sized from the segment's doc count, and you expect lookups of absent keys to be rejected quickly in every segment. For a segment of 226,279,579 docs or more, FuzzySet.createOptimalSet's int expression 2 * setSize wraps negative, the size lookup falls back to its smallest size (63) and the hash count rounds to 0, so the filter has 64 bits, never sets one and answers MAYBE for every key, and the saturation check meant to retire useless filters sees 0% saturation and saves it. Results stay correct, but every absent-key lookup on that segment goes to the terms dictionary: the repro's filter rejects 0 of 1,000 absent keys, while one doc fewer gives a 2^30-bit filter with 3 hash functions that rejected 2,000 of 2,000 in an independent test.

bugs.area: codecs / IndexedDISI jump table (presence sets of sparse doc values, norms and vectors)
bugs.title: IndexedDISI returns its jump-table entry count as a signed short, so a sparse doc-values, norms or vector field whose last doc id is >= 2,147,352,576 stores a negative count and every reader ignores the jump table that was written (advance walks block by block; results stay correct)
bugs.summary: You build a segment of more than 2,147,352,576 documents with the default codec, with a doc-values, norms or vector field that some documents lack and that a document near the end of the doc-id range has. You expect the field's index-time jump table (added in 8.0 'for O(1) advance') to be used, so that advance to a far document jumps straight to its 65,536-doc block. Instead IndexedDISI.writeBitSet writes 32,768 or 32,769 table entries but returns their count as a short (-32,768 or -32,767), the codec stores that value, and every reader treats a negative count as 'no jump table', so advance and advanceExact walk the block headers one by one; the documents and values returned stay correct.

bugs.title: BBoxStrategy's overlap-ratio explanation (BBoxOverlapRatioValueSource) shows the target ratio under 'queryFactor' instead of the query ratio, so explain misreports how the score was computed; the score itself is correct
bugs.summary: You score documents with BBoxStrategy.makeOverlapRatioValueSource and call explain, and you expect the tree to show the terms of the documented formula, queryFactor = queryRatio * queryTargetProportion and targetFactor = targetRatio * (1 - queryTargetProportion). Instead the 'ratio' child of the 'queryFactor' node, printed next to 'area of <query box>', is targetRatio, the same number as under 'targetFactor': for the query box x[0,20] y[0,10] and the document box x[10,40] y[5,15] at proportion 0.3 it shows 0.16666667 (50/300) where queryRatio is 0.25 (50/200). The score (0.19166666) and the queryFactor value (0.075) are right; one token on line 255 is wrong, a slip from the 2015 LUCENE-6446 Explanation API rewrite, and 5.1.0 still showed queryRatio.

bugs.area: core / search similarities (Axiomatic F1/F3 term-frequency explanation, tfExplain)
bugs.title: AxiomaticF1EXP, F1LOG, F3EXP and F3LOG explain tf as 'computed as 1 + log(1 + log(freq))' of the raw freq, but the value they show is 1 + log(1 + log(freq + 1)); the score itself is correct
bugs.summary: You search with AxiomaticF1EXP (or F1LOG, F3EXP, F3LOG) and call IndexSearcher.explain on a hit. The tf node says 'tf, term frequency computed as 1 + log(1 + log(freq)) from:' and its only child is 'freq, number of occurrences of term in the document', the raw count, so you expect its value to be that formula of that child. Instead tf first adds 1 to freq (since LUCENE-8010, 2017), so for freq = 1 the node shows 1.5265890 where the stated formula gives 1.0, and for freq = 3 it shows 1.8697417 instead of 1.7412763; the score is right and only the formula text is stale.

bugs.area: analysis / Thai (ThaiRepeatFilter offset split; ThaiAnalyzer with ThaiCharFilter, or a custom chain with HTMLStripCharFilter)
bugs.title: ThaiRepeatFilter gives the repeated word the offsets of a deleted character or of the following markup instead of the Maiyamok's, when a CharFilter removed characters right after the Maiyamok (a zero-width space in the default ThaiAnalyzer, a closing tag with HTMLStripCharFilter)
bugs.summary: You analyze 'บ่อยๆ' + U+200B + 'ครับ' (a word written with the repetition mark ๆ, then a zero-width space) with the stock ThaiAnalyzer and expect what happens without the zero-width space, and what the filter's CHANGES entry promises ('exact OffsetAttribute and highlighter compatibility'): the base token บ่อย covers the word [0,4) and the repeated token บ่อย covers the ๆ [4,5). Instead the base token gets [0,5), which includes the ๆ, and the repeated token gets [5,6), which is only the removed zero-width space: ThaiRepeatFilter assumes that the last characters of the token's offset span are its trailing ๆ, but the CharFilter's offset correction put the removed character at the end of that span. With HTMLStripCharFilter the repeated token points at the last character of the tag after the word instead, so a highlighter writes its markup inside the tag; terms and positions are correct and nothing fails.

bugs.area: analysis / nori KoreanTokenizer (Viterbi decompound backtrace; UserDictionary and bundled-dictionary compounds)
bugs.title: KoreanTokenizer gives the parts of a decompounded word offsets counted back from the end of the word while their text is cut from the start of the word, so when the parts do not cover the whole word (a user-dictionary entry with a shorter segmentation such as '세종시 세종', or 7 compounds of the bundled dictionary such as 픽토그램) the offsets point at other characters (픽토 at [1,3) covers '토그')
bugs.summary: You analyze text containing 픽토그램 ('pictogram') with the default KoreanAnalyzer, or 세종시 with the user dictionary entry '세종시 세종', and expect each decompounded part's offsets to cover the characters its text came from, as they do when the parts cover the whole word (가락지나물 gives 가락지[0,3) and 나물[3,5)). Instead nori cuts each part's text from the start of the word but counts its offsets back from the end of the word, so 픽토그램 gives 픽토[1,3), covering '토그', and 그[3,4), covering '램', and '세종시 세종' gives 세종[1,3), covering '종시'; highlighters mark the wrong characters. Lucene accepts both inputs without a check: UserDictionary rejects only a segmentation longer than the word, and 7 compounds in the bundled dictionary have parts that do not add up to the word.

bugs.area: monitor / HighlightsMatch on batches (DocumentBatch: MultiDocumentBatch keeps the caller's FieldType, SingletonDocumentBatch uses MemoryIndex with offsets)
bugs.title: Monitor HighlightsMatch returns -1 offsets for a TextField document matched in a batch of two or more documents, but the real offsets when the same document is matched alone; the upstream batch test expects the offsets but cannot notice, because Hit.compareTo ignores offsets
bugs.summary: You register a query with a Monitor and match a document whose text is in a plain TextField with HighlightsMatch.MATCHER; each hit carries its positions and character offsets (the phrase "cell biology" in 'the cell biology count' is positions 1-2, offsets 4-16). Match the same document in a batch of two or more documents with Monitor.match(Document) and the hits keep the right positions, but both offsets are -1, because a single document goes into a MemoryIndex that always stores offsets while a batch is indexed with the documents' own field types, and TextField indexes no offsets. The module's own test testHighlightBatches expects the real offsets in a batch (Hit(1, 4, 2, 16)) but cannot notice, because the hit set's contains uses Hit.compareTo, which ignores offsets (the sibling bug LFV-915).

bugs.area: analysis / char filters (MappingCharFilter, BaseCharFilter offset correction)
bugs.title: MappingCharFilter.reset rewinds the input but keeps the offset corrections recorded on the first pass, so after a reset and re-read correctOffset (and the token offsets a Tokenizer derives from it) are wrong, or BaseCharFilter's ordering assertion fires
bugs.summary: You read a MappingCharFilter to the end, call reset to rewind it (MappingCharFilter overrides reset for this, and upstream TestMappingCharFilter.testReaderReset re-reads after it), read it again and expect correctOffset to map the second pass's output back to the input exactly as on the first pass. Instead reset rewinds the input and the filter's read state but not the offset-correction map it inherits from BaseCharFilter, so the second pass appends new corrections computed from the first pass's last cumulative diff: for the map a->xy over "a", correctOffset(2) returns 0 instead of 1, and a WhitespaceTokenizer over the re-read filter for "a b" gives xy[0,0] b[1,2] instead of xy[0,1] b[2,3]. For deleting or shrinking maps, with -ea the second read trips BaseCharFilter's 'Offset... is less than the last recorded offset' assertion, and with -da it returns offsets past the end of the input (b->'' over "ba": correctOffset(1) = 3 for a 2-character input).
bugs.introduced_commit: 6a3752feb8f13541603e85326db997147047b2a6 (svn r791415), LUCENE-1734 'CharReader should delegate reset/mark/markSupported' (apache/lucene#2808; a JIRA patch from the svn era, no GitHub PR), committed by uschindler for an issue reported by kojisekig: it removed MappingCharFilter's reset that threw 'mark/reset not supported' and made reset delegate to the input, and no commit since has cleared BaseCharFilter's correction list [exec]. The current reset override (rewinds input, buffer, replacement and inputOff, not the map) comes from LUCENE-3830 (3e9b5a9893c, apache/lucene#4903, 2012-05-06, first release 4.0.0), which made the defect visible on a plain read to EOF for most inputs [read]

bugs.area: highlighter / matchhighlight: PassageFormatter multi-marker formatting (crossing markers with per-marker end strings; also end to end through MatchHighlighter, FieldValueHighlighters.highlighted and MatchHighlighter.QueryOffsetRange)
bugs.title: matchhighlight PassageFormatter closes crossing markers in opening order instead of innermost first, so per-marker end strings come out mis-nested (e.g. 'one two three' instead of 'one two three')
bugs.summary: You format the passage 'one two three' with two crossing markers, [0,7) written as ... and [4,13) as ..., using PassageFormatter's Function constructor, or you highlight the crossing phrase queries 'one two' and 'two three' with MatchHighlighter.highlight(topDocs, q1, q2) and one tag per query. You expect well-nested output, 'one two three', because when a marker ends the formatter closes and re-opens the markers opened after it precisely to resolve the overlap into nested markup (Passage javadoc: markers 'can be overlapping or nested'). Instead it closes those markers in opening order rather than innermost first and returns 'one two three' (end to end 'one two three'), which an XML parser rejects.

bugs.area: highlighter / matchhighlight: PassageSelector passage windows and long-match truncation, BreakIteratorShrinkingAdjuster (through FieldValueHighlighters.maxLeadingCharacters and highlighted)
bugs.title: matchhighlight PassageSelector can cut a passage or a truncated match between the two halves of a supplementary character, so FieldValueHighlighters.maxLeadingCharacters and highlighted return a snippet with an unpaired surrogate
bugs.summary: You highlight a stored value with matchhighlight's FieldValueHighlighters, for example maxLeadingCharacters(5, '...', fields) on a value that starts with the word BOLD written in mathematical bold capitals (U+1D401 U+1D40E U+1D40B U+1D403, two UTF-16 units each), or highlighted(5,...) with a term query that matches that word. You expect a snippet of whole characters within the 5-unit budget, for example the first two letters and '...', just as the ASCII value 'boldtext' is cut inside the word but between characters ('boldt...'). Instead the snippet ends with the first half of the third letter ('\uD835\uDC01\uD835\uDC0E\uD835...' and '>\uD835\uDC01\uD835\uDC0E\uD835<...'), because PassageSelector cuts windows and long matches at a raw UTF-16 offset and BreakIteratorShrinkingAdjuster keeps that raw edge when no word boundary fits in the window.

bugs.area: core / util AttributeSource (removeAllAttributes and the cached State chain, getCurrentState / currentState[0])
bugs.title: AttributeSource.removeAllAttributes leaves the cached State chain in place, so until the next addAttribute captureState/restoreState, copyTo, hashCode, the impls iterator, reflection and clearAttributes/endAttributes still act on the removed attributes
bugs.summary: You call removeAllAttributes on an AttributeSource (for example a token stream you reuse with a different set of attributes) after it has been used, for example by clearAttributes, which every Tokenizer calls for each token. You expect it to behave like a new, empty source until you add attributes again, as hasAttributes (false) and equals (equal to a new AttributeSource) already say. Instead the method clears its two maps but not the cached chain of attribute instances that captureState, copyTo, hashCode, the impls iterator, reflection and clearAttributes/endAttributes walk, so until the next addAttribute they still see the removed attributes: restoreState(captureState) on the same source throws IllegalArgumentException, hashCode differs from that of an equal empty source, and reflectAsString still prints 'term=foo,...'.

bugs.area: queryparser / flexible (AbstractRangeQueryNode.toQueryString, PointQueryNode.getTermEscaped, the StandardSyntaxParser range lexer, the open-bound forms of OpenRangeQueryNodeProcessor and PointRangeQueryNodeProcessor, BooleanQueryNodeBuilder)
bugs.title: Flexible query parser: AbstractRangeQueryNode.toQueryString does not keep the 11.0 'can be parsed back' promise for quoted bounds that contain a space, ']' or '}' or for open bounds in processed trees, and an open point bound makes it throw IllegalArgumentException, which escapes StandardQueryParser.parse at the clause limit
bugs.summary: You parse a range such as f:["a b" TO c] or f:[a TO *] with the flexible StandardQueryParser, call toQueryString on the range node and parse the result again, as the 11.0 CHANGES entry for #7865 says you can. Instead a bound with a space, ']' or '}' prints backslash-escaped (f:[a\ b TO c]), which the range lexer rejects even for the syntax parser's own node; a processed open term bound prints as nothing (f:[a TO ]); and a processed open point bound (i:[1 TO *] with a PointsConfig) makes toQueryString and toString throw IllegalArgumentException 'Cannot format given Object as a Number'. Because BooleanQueryNodeBuilder builds its too-many-clauses message with toQueryString, a query over the clause limit that contains such an open point range makes StandardQueryParser.parse throw that IllegalArgumentException instead of the documented QueryNodeException, in every release since 4.0.
bugs.introduced_commit: Round-trip failures: 17ca89d52fa96138518182b32d5de48940a2d977 (apache/lucene#14697 'Fix AbstractRangeQueryNode#toQueryString', by GitHub phb-ig, merged by stefanvodita, fixing #7865 / LUCENE-6807), an incomplete fix that created the parse-back promise, not a regression (before it no range round-tripped at all) [read]. bugs.area: queryparser / complexPhrase: ComplexPhraseQueryParser (pass-2 same-field check for clauses nested in a phrase)
bugs.title: ComplexPhraseQueryParser skips its same-field check for prefix and regular-expression clauses: "jo* id:2*" parses and then fails at search time with IllegalArgumentException, and name:"id:2*" searches field id
bugs.summary: You parse a quoted phrase such as "jo* id:2*" or "jo* id:/2/" with ComplexPhraseQueryParser on the default field name; its class javadoc says the second pass checks that all embedded clauses refer to the same field, and it rejects "jo* id:2", "jo* id:2?", "jo* id:2~1" and "jo* id:[1 TO 2]" at parse time, so you expect a parse error. Instead parse succeeds, because the check is wired into newTermQuery, getWildcardQuery, getRangeQuery and getFuzzyQuery but the class never overrides getPrefixQuery or getRegexpQuery, and the search then throws IllegalArgumentException 'Clauses must have same field.'. A one-clause phrase such as name:"id:2*" also parses, and because rewrite returns a lone multi-term query unchanged, it searches field id and returns the document whose id is 2.

The regexp forms come from 838e19beae1f (LUCENE-2604, #3678, 2010-08-30), which added regexp syntax and QueryParser.getRegexpQuery without an override in this class. The one-clause search on the other field comes from LUCENE-7614 (#8665; 52f2a77b78fc on master, backport ac85a41cbefa on branch_6x, 2017-01-05), whose rewrite fast path returns a lone MultiTermQuery unchanged; before it, the one-clause form threw 'Unknown query type' at search.
